verdict.summary: In imgdir mode, num_images (unsigned 32-bit, line 60) is never capped; the allocation expression `num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(char)` at line 63 wraps, so with >= 2^32/OPJ_PATH_LEN directory entries (1,048,577 when OPJ_PATH_LEN is 4096) the filename_buf allocation collapses to 4096 bytes while the loop at line 71 derives slot pointers up to ~4 GB out of range and load_images at line 74 writes file names into them, yielding a heap buffer overflow (primary CWE-122, secondary CWE-190). A second candidate, double free of l_stream across loop iterations, is plausible but not confirmable from the shown code alone.

evidence.snippet:
dirptr->filename_buf = (char*)malloc(num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(
                    char)); /* Stores at max 10 image file names*/
evidence.reason: The malloc size is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic from num_images, whose residual range (line 60) is unconstrained by any shown cap. For num_images = 2^32/OPJ_PATH_LEN + 1 (1,048,577 with OPJ_PATH_LEN = 4096), the product wraps to 4096, so malloc receives a wrapped, far-too-small size (CWE-190); the same wrapped offset arithmetic at line 71 later feeds out-of-range slot pointers to the write at line 74, making the resulting heap overflow a CWE-122. The value passes every guard on the path: line 59 (set_imgdir == 1), line 62 (dirptr != NULL), line 66 (filename_buf != NULL), line 70 (i < num_images admits i up to 1,048,576).

With the wrapped 4096-byte allocation from line 63, iteration i = 1,048,575 derives the pointer filename_buf + 4,294,963,200 (unsigned 32-bit stride, no wrap at that i), approximately 4 GB beyond the allocation; the loop bound `i < num_images` admits this index, and the derived pointer is consumed as a write destination by load_images at line 74, producing the out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-122, caused by the CWE-190 wrap at line 63).

Call-site confirmation of the overflow sink: by its name and the slot convention fixed in the shown code (per-entry capacity OPJ_PATH_LEN from lines 63-64 and stride i * OPJ_PATH_LEN from line 71), load_images writes each file name into dirptr->filename[i], i.e., into the buffer at the out-of-range pointers derived at line 71. For num_images = 1,048,577 the buffer is only 4096 bytes while paths land at offsets up to 4,294,963,200, so the writes corrupt the heap (primary CWE-122; the 32-bit wrap of the allocation size at line 63 is the independently confirmed root cause, CWE-190).

assumptions: OPJ_PATH_LEN expands to 4096 and unsigned int is 32 bits, which yields the concrete witness 1,048,577; the overflow-triggering count of 2^32/OPJ_PATH_LEN + 1 generalizes for any OPJ_PATH_LEN <= 2^32.
malloc returns at least the requested (wrapped) byte count, so the 4096-byte allocation succeeds and passes the check at line 66.

get_num_images returns the directory entry count (or -1 on error), and the attacker can populate the directory, making `num_images` attacker-influenced with an unbounded residual range in the shown code.

load_images, per its name and the shown directory-slot conventions (per-slot size OPJ_PATH_LEN, stride i * OPJ_PATH_LEN), stores file paths of at most OPJ_PATH_LEN bytes into the provided buffer slots.
limitations: NULL dereference of dirptr->filename (lines 65/71): requires the unchecked malloc at line 65 to fail; allocation-failure-only, not confirmed as attacker-triggerable.

Possible double-free/use-after-free of l_stream: destroyed at line 370 after a successful iteration and, without reassignment to NULL, destroyed again at line 264 in the cod_format default branch on a later loop iteration; reachability depends on unshown get_next_file/parse behavior varying cod_format between iterations, so it is not confirmable from the shown code alone.

If get_num_images returns -1, num_images becomes 0xFFFFFFFF (line 60) causing ~4 GB / ~34 GB allocations and then the NULL-deref path above; requires opendir failure and is an allocation-pressure/DoS-only concern.
load_images return is compared only against `== 1` (line 74); other nonzero error codes would proceed, but no security impact is demonstrable from the shown code.
The IMF mainlevel indexing (lines 215-239) is safely guarded: the guard admits 1..11 and the array has 12 elements, so no OOB is possible there.
All fprintf format strings are literals; no format-string, SQL, command, or log injection sink exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only path that could corrupt memory is the frame-size derivation at lines 41-46, where an attacker-controlled 32-bit size is summed into an allocation and read length; the guard at line 42 (size > 0xFFFFFF -> reject) admits only size in [0, 0xFFFFFF], so size + DXA_EXTRA_SIZE + pal_size <= 16,777,996 cannot wrap in uint32/int, and all derived memcpy/avio_read offsets (lines 48-49, and 25-29, 36-37, 54) stay within their allocated objects. Remaining concerns (discarded short-read/seek returns producing stale or uninitialized stack bytes, and a large-but-capped 16 MB per-frame allocation) are robustness/DoS-volume issues whose volume is not confirmable from the shown code and cause no out-of-bounds access.

assumptions: DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is a macro defined outside the shown snippet; standard FFmpeg defines it as 9, which makes the AV_RB32(buf + 5) read at line 41 (bytes buf[5..8]) in-bounds. The shown code itself does not expose the buffer capacity.
Fields readvid, has_sound, bytes_left, bpc, wavpos, vidpos, and frames come from header parsing outside the shown code; only constraints visible in the shown code were used in the analysis.
limitations: Return values of avio_read at lines 22, 37, 40 and avio_seek at lines 10, 20 are discarded. A truncated attacker file can leave parts of buf/pal stale or uninitialized, so the 4-byte tag (line 23) and frame size (line 41) can be derived from stale bytes; however, any derived size still must pass the line-42 cap (<= 0xFFFFFF), so the worst outcome is a transient allocation of up to ~16,777,996 bytes followed by ret != size -> av_free_packet + AVERROR(EIO) (lines 49-53), with no out-of-bounds access.

Per-frame allocation up to ~16 MB at line 46 is attacker-influenced but capped and must be matched by real file data read at line 49; repeated-call volume depends on c->frames, whose provenance is outside the shown code, so no resource-exhaustion finding is confirmed.
The safety of AV_RB32(buf + 5) at line 41 depends on DXA_EXTRA_SIZE >= 9, which cannot be verified from the shown code alone (macro not defined in the snippet).

The historical integer-overflow/heap-overflow pattern that motivated this FRAM code is present in design but fully excluded by the line-42 guard; it is recorded here only as a fixed/guarded concern, not a finding.

verdict.summary: The shown fallback branch explicitly admits base_dir_name == NULL (lines 49-71), but base_dir_name is then used unguarded at line 113 in concat_path_file(base_dir_name, problem_id) after the dump directory has been fully populated. The helper's first argument is, by name and use, a non-NULL path string that it dereferences/concatenates, so the shown code passes NULL to a string-consuming operation: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476), or on glibc's lenient %s handling a wrong '(null)' rename path consumed by dd_rename at line 115. Low severity (DoS / dump-misplacement logic flaw; no memory corruption or privilege impact).

evidence.reason: base_dir_name is an internal-helper parameter whose residual range after the only guard touching it (the branch at lines 49-51) still includes NULL, because the else-path (lines 51-71) is executed exactly when base_dir_name == NULL and no later check exists. Witness: base_dir_name == NULL with try_dd_create succeeding at line 54 (or 63/70), so dd != NULL (line 73 satisfied), the loop and dd_create_basic_files complete, and control reaches line 113 with base_dir_name still NULL. concat_path_file's first argument is, by its name and use in the shown code, a path string the helper dereferences, so NULL is an out-of-domain argument: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) inside the helper, or at minimum a wrong '(null)'<problem_id> rename target handed to dd_rename at line 115, relocating the populated dump directory to an unintended path.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the start of the pasted snippet.

NEW_PD_SUFFIX expands to a non-empty string literal (e.g. "-new"), so the index strlen(problem_id) - strlen(NEW_PD_SUFFIX) at line 112 is in-bounds because line 44's format literal ends with that suffix.

str_is_correct_filename, per its name, rejects '/', '\', whitespace/control characters and directory components (body not shown), so type (line 13) and name (line 82) cannot carry path separators; the traversal-safety conclusion relies on that name-implied semantics.
uid_t is a 32-bit unsigned type (Linux), which determines the value produced by the cast at line 34.
xasprintf and the x* helpers abort on allocation failure, so their results are treated as non-NULL.
problem_data is a GHashTable whose keys/values are non-NULL in normal use; the shown code dereferences value->flags at line 88 without a NULL check on value.
limitations: Negative uid strings such as "-2" pass the line-28 guard (no lower-bound check; INT_MAX < val bounds only the top), giving uid = (uid_t)(-2) = 4294967294 at line 34, consumed by try_dd_create (lines 50/54/63/70) and dd_create_basic_files (line 110); no security impact beyond invalid file ownership/DoS is demonstrable from the shown code, and the FILENAME_UID item is normally populated by the tool itself, so no CWE is attached.
Whether concat_path_file crashes on a NULL first argument or substitutes "(null)" depends on its unshown body (glibc prints "(null)" for NULL %s); the out-of-domain NULL argument itself is confirmed.
dd_rename's return value at line 115 is discarded, so a failed rename is treated as success (CWE-703-class); impact is a leftover '-new'-suffixed dump directory — robustness only.
Line 46 passes base_dir_name (possibly NULL) to log_info's %s and prints uid_t with %d; line 96 prints unsigned long with %li — C undefined behavior that is benign on glibc, no impact demonstrated.

For CD_FLAG_BIN items, copy_file(value->content, dest, DEFAULT_DUMP_DIR_MODE | S_IROTH) at line 92 copies an attacker-influenceable source path into the dump and creates the copy world-readable; whether this leaks data depends on the dump-directory mode and on problem-data trust, neither visible in the shown code.

value->content is logged at lines 91/94 without newline filtering; a crafted path containing '\n' could inject log lines, but the log consumer and the ability to control bin-item content are outside the shown code.
type and hash keys have no length cap; adversarial maximum lengths can cause ENAMETOOLONG failures or oversized log lines (DoS), but xasprintf bounds its allocation, so there is no memory unsafety.

verdict.summary: copy_file_content calls strcpy(out, buf) (line 28) on a buf that is not guaranteed NUL-terminated: type=security fills the post-prefix region with 0x07 (line 22) and read() (line 20) overwrites the terminator with arbitrary file bytes, so any file content lacking a NUL byte (even an empty file) makes strcpy copy past the 1024-byte stack array out — a stack buffer overflow with attacker-controlled length and content, plus an accompanying OOB read of buf.

evidence.reason: Unbounded strcpy with no length bound. Sink input buf is tainted by entry-point file bytes (read at line 20) and by the 0x07 fill selected by the entry-point string type (line 22), which destroys the snprintf terminator at buf[14]. The only guard before the sink, count < 0 (line 21), admits count = 3 (file 'ABC', no NUL): buf[0..1023] then contains no NUL byte, so strcpy writes out[0..1023] and beyond the 1024-byte stack array declared at main line 14, and reads buf[1024] past buf's same capacity — primary CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow.

assumptions: out and buf are fixed-size stack arrays of exactly BUF_SIZE = 1024 bytes, per main lines 11-14.
read() may return fewer bytes than requested; the overflow witness holds for count in [0, 1010] when a NUL byte is absent from buf.
limitations: Descriptor leak: fd is only closed on the read-error path (line 23); the success path never closes it — single-shot, not compounded by attacker-controlled volume in the shown program.
remaining = BUF_SIZE - 14 (line 19) would be negative for BUF_SIZE < 14, but the only shown call site passes 1024 (line 29), so an underflow is not reachable in the shown code.
Functional mode overflow needs the file to supply 1010 consecutive non-NUL bytes (count == 1010); the security-mode witness with a short non-NUL file is the demonstrated path.
out[BUF_SIZE - 1] = '\0' (line 31) executes only after the overflow has already happened and cannot mitigate it.
Truncation is ignored: strcpy stops at the first NUL in file content; no security impact.
O_RDONLY open without O_NOFOLLOW permits symlink following, but no privilege boundary or authorization mechanism exists in the shown code to make this a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: get_ls_result returns pointers to the static string literal "" on its error paths (lines 20, 25, 48), and main unconditionally calls free(output) at line 83 on whatever the function returned at line 78. Freeing a pointer to non-heap static memory violates free()'s required domain and is undefined behavior (CWE-590), typically ending in an allocator abort or heap corruption (DoS). The trigger is an OS resource failure (pipe/fork/realloc) rather than a value of dir_path, which limits attacker control but does not remove the defect.

evidence.reason: Sink: free() consumes the value returned by get_ls_result at line 78. The returned pointer's residual range includes the static string literal "" produced by the error branches at lines 20, 25, and 48 (the guards at lines 19, 24, and 46 admit those branches and return the literal with no marker or validation, and the argc == 2 guard at line 73 admits that result into the sink path). free() requires an allocator-returned pointer; passing a pointer to static read-only memory is out of domain at the call site, causing undefined behavior — typically 'free(): invalid pointer' abort (CWE-590).

assumptions: argv[1] is non-NULL whenever argc == 2, per standard main() semantics.
read() returns at most the requested count (255 with buffer[256]) and returns 0 at EOF, -1 on error; the child closes all pipe write-end copies before exiting, so EOF is eventually delivered.
limitations: The trigger for the confirmed free-of-literal is OS resource failure (pipe(), fork(), or realloc() failing), which is not directly controllable via the dir_path input; attacker-triggerability is environmental (e.g., EMFILE under file-descriptor exhaustion).

On realloc failure (lines 45-48) the previously accumulated heap buffer is leaked because the old pointer is overwritten by NULL before the return; this is a single-shot leak per invocation and is treated as a robustness concern.

read() returning -1 is indistinguishable from EOF at line 44, so a read error yields a truncated buffer null-terminated at line 57 and returned as success at line 66 — an output-integrity/error-handling flaw (CWE-754-style) with no privilege boundary.
The return statuses of dup2() (line 29) and waitpid() (line 64) are discarded; impacts (stdout not redirected on dup2 failure, unreaped children) are minor robustness concerns.
strdup("") at line 59 could return NULL only under memory exhaustion, making printf("%s", output) at line 80 receive NULL; failure of a 2-byte allocation is not attacker-controllable.
The realloc size expression output_size + bytes_read + 1 at line 45 can only overflow after roughly 2^64 bytes of ls output, which is not reachable in practice.

A dir_path beginning with '-' is passed positionally to ls and may be parsed as an option (e.g., "-R"); execlp does not invoke a shell so there is no command injection, and ls options only affect the invoking user's own listing — a behavior deviation, not a confirmed vulnerability.
execlp resolves 'ls' via PATH at line 32; the environment is not part of the shown code and the program runs with the invoking user's privileges, so PATH substitution is out of scope.

verdict.summary: dupstr is a standard, correct string-duplication helper: the allocation size (strlen(src)+1, line 3) exactly matches the number of bytes the NUL-terminated copy loop (line 9) writes, malloc's return is checked (line 4) with a well-formed error path (lines 5-6), and the fprintf format string is fully literal. Residual concerns (NULL or non-NUL-terminated src) depend on caller-provided invariants not established or producible inside the shown code, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: src is a valid pointer to a NUL-terminated string, which is the contract implied by the use of strlen(src) at line 3; this invariant is not established anywhere in the shown code.
The copy-loop bound is derived from the same strlen(src) value used to size the allocation, making the destination write range self-consistent when the string contract holds.
limitations: Passing a NULL src would invoke undefined behavior at strlen(src) (line 3); NULL is not produced anywhere in the shown code and can only arrive from an out-of-scope caller, so the NULL-dereference standard requires this to remain a limitation (no CWE).

Passing a non-NUL-terminated src would cause an out-of-bounds read in strlen (line 3) and in the copy loop (line 9); the capacity of src's object is not identifiable from the shown code, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable (no CWE).
A size_t wrap in strlen(src)+1 would require strlen to return SIZE_MAX, which is not realizable for any addressable object; no integer-overflow finding is confirmed.
The allocated buffer is never freed inside the helper; this is a single-shot ownership hand-off to the caller, not a volume-compounding leak, and is out of scope.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The only arithmetic/allocation sink is PackedArray::MakeReserve(args.size() + 1) at line 5, which is a capacity hint: a theoretical SIZE_MAX wrap would produce a smaller (0) reserve, not an oversized allocation, and the shown code performs no unchecked stores based on that size. The VarEnv pointer from getOrCreateVarEnv() is NULL-guarded at line 7 before the helper calls, so no NULL dereference is reachable. All actual parsing/storage occurs inside the unshown compact(...) helper, which is outside the scope of this analysis.

assumptions: PackedArray::MakeReserve(n) and subsequent appends by the hidden compact(...) helper follow standard packed-array growth semantics, so a smaller reserve cannot cause out-of-bounds writes in the shown code.
args is a PHP Array whose element count is bounded by framework construction limits; an Array with 2^64-1 elements is not producible, but this invariant is not visible in the shown code.
limitations: Potential integer overflow in args.size() + 1 (line 5) requires args.size() == SIZE_MAX, which is not reachable via any mechanism shown, and even a wrap to 0 is consumed only as a capacity hint with no failure-producing sink; no CWE attached.
The body of the recursive compact(...) helper (lines 9-10) is not shown; any parsing, storage, or recursion-depth behavior there cannot be confirmed or refuted from the shown code.
The semantics of raise_disallowed_dynamic_call (line 4) — throwing versus continuing — do not affect safety of the shown code either way and are not analyzed as a finding.
No resource-exhaustion or ReDoS claim is made because the only iteration/recursion is inside the unshown helper and no bound or sink is identifiable in the shown code.

verdict.summary: nfs3svc_decode_writeargs splits attacker-controlled len across rqstp->rq_vec[]/rq_pages[] in the loop at lines 47-52 with no bound on v. len can remain at 0xFFFFFFFF (count==len at line 20 admits it; XDR_QUADLEN(0xFFFFFFFF)*4 wraps to 0 at line 37 so the receive check passes even with no data; the cap at line 40 is bypassed by equality with max_blocksize, which the shown code never constrains), driving v to ~2^20 and writing rqstp->rq_vec[v] past the array (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write).

evidence.reason: Index v originates from the entry-point length: len/count are ntohl() decoded at lines 14-16, pass count==len (line 20) and the wrapped dlen check (line 37) with witness count=len=max_blocksize=0xFFFFFFFF, so line 40's cap is not taken (0xFFFFFFFF > 0xFFFFFFFF is false). The loop then increments v roughly len/PAGE_SIZE ~ 2^20 times with no v-capacity guard, and this statement writes rqstp->rq_vec[v] and reads rqstp->rq_pages[v] with that unbounded index, causing an out-of-bounds write (primary CWE-787).

Same unbounded v from the len/count/max_blocksize residual range [0, 0xFFFFFFFF] writes rqstp->rq_vec[v].iov_len each loop iteration; with the witness above, v reaches ~1,048,575 and this write lands beyond the fixed rq_vec[] member array of struct svc_rqst (CWE-787). The shown code contains no v-bound check, and XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 == 0 for len in {0xFFFFFFFD..0xFFFFFFFF} admits the huge len at line 37.

Post-loop write of rqstp->rq_vec[v] with the same unbounded index v (residual range ~ [0, 2^20-1] derived from attacker len/max_blocksize), executing after the loop exits; for the witness len=max_blocksize=0xFFFFFFFF this is an out-of-bounds write to the fixed rq_vec[] array (primary CWE-787), since no capacity guard exists between line 5 and line 53.

assumptions: PAGE_SIZE is the standard Linux 4096-byte page constant, used to estimate the maximum reachable index ~ len/4096.
rqstp->rq_vec[] and rqstp->rq_pages[] are fixed-size member arrays of struct svc_rqst of some finite capacity; that numeric capacity is not declared anywhere in the shown code.
limitations: The exact numeric capacity of rqstp->rq_vec[]/rq_pages[] is not identifiable from the shown code, so the precise excess (index - capacity) cannot be stated as an exact number; the finding rests on the shown code's own arithmetic producing v ~ 2^20 with no bound guard and on the unconstrained residual range [0, 0xFFFFFFFF] of max_blocksize.

head->iov_len - hdr at line 45 can underflow if p lies past head->iov_base + head->iov_len, but that requires a header-fitting invariant established outside the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.
The 64-bit to 32-bit narrowing of dlen at line 28 could mis-evaluate the receive check for receives larger than 4 GiB; transport maxima are outside the shown code.
xdr_decode_hyper()'s return at line 12 is not checked before dereference at lines 14-16, but a NULL-producing failure mode is not visible within the shown code.

If an out-of-snippet invariant caps max_blocksize at 1 MiB, the overflow depends on whether v ~ 256 exceeds the unshown rq_vec[] capacity at that boundary; that specific boundary is unconfirmable from the snippet.
If the declared length exceeds the data actually received, the consuming write path (outside the shown code) would read pages that were never populated; that OOB data read occurs in unshown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The only copy sink is headerPut(h,&td,HEADERPUT_DEFAULT) at line 69, and every argument it receives is produced by headerNext (line 7) and then bounded by explicit guards in the shown code: scalar/integer types are admitted only when td.count == 1 (lines 56-58), string/string-array/bin types only when td.count < 16*1024 (lines 62-64), and unknown tags only when in [HEADER_SIGBASE, HEADER_TAGBASE) (line 42). The shown code performs no size, index, or pointer arithmetic, so no out-of-domain value reaches the sink. The discarded headerPut return (line 69), the unchecked headerInitIterator result (line 6), and all memory-safety concerns about headerPut/headerNext internals lack impact or a capacity/dangerous-derivation anchor inside the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: td.tag, td.type, td.count and td.data are filled by headerNext(hi,&td) before the body runs (line 7 guards the body), and headerNext returns nonzero only for a valid entry.
td.count is an unsigned 32-bit count (rpm_count_t) as in rpm's public headers; the guarded comparisons at lines 56 and 62 are therefore well-defined against the literals 1 and 16*1024.
headerPut copies the entry data into h (standard header-insert semantics), so freeing td.data in the loop increment (line 7) does not leave h referencing freed memory.
headerIsEntry(h,td.tag) is a membership test with no side effects relevant to safety.
headerInitIterator/headerNext/headerFreeIterator operate over a finite entry set and terminate.
limitations: OOB read/write in headerPut at line 69 cannot be confirmed: the object capacity for td.data (the byte length or number of NUL-terminated strings actually present) is an invariant of headerNext's parser, not identifiable from the shown code, and the shown code derives no size/index that exceeds it (count is capped to 0..16383 or required to be 1).

headerPut's return value is discarded at line 69 via (void); a failed merge silently omits the entry and the loop continues (line 7) then frees the iterator (line 72). Impact on any security mechanism (e.g., signature presence downstream) is not visible in the shown code, so this is only a CWE-754-style robustness concern.
headerInitIterator(sigh) at line 6 is not checked for NULL before use at lines 7 and 72; a NULL can only arise from an allocation failure inside the unshown callee, not from the shown code.
NULL h or sigh would only come from a caller; no shown path produces NULL.

For RPM_STRING_TYPE/RPM_STRING_ARRAY_TYPE, count is capped at line 62 but the shown code does not (and cannot, from visible data) verify that td.data contains that many NUL-terminated elements; that check belongs to the unshown parser.

The signedness of td.count is not declared in the shown code. If it were signed (rpm actually uses uint32_t), a negative count could pass line 62 and convert to a huge size in headerPut (CWE-195-style); because the type is not visible here, no witness can be expressed with the shown code's own types.
Tag translation (lines 12-33) preserves the source td.type; a mismatched type stored into h could confuse downstream readers, but all such consumers are outside the shown code.
Caller-side aliasing (h == sigh) could invalidate the iterator mid-iteration; that condition is not shown.

When headerNext returns zero, the final rpmtdFreeData (line 7) does not run, leaking the last entry's data once per header; this single-shot leak does not compound with attacker-controlled volume in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Double-free of `copy` in `split`: `copy` is freed at line 20, then the failure path of the terminating-NULL `realloc` at line 23 frees it again at line 29. The branch is entered when at least one token was parsed (`if (i)` at line 22 admits i >= 1) and the final realloc fails; the requested size 8*(i+1) grows with the attacker-controlled token count of `arg`, so the allocation failure and the resulting heap double-free can be induced with a sufficiently large delimiter-separated input.

evidence.reason: CWE-415 double-free: `copy` is a heap object (from `dupstr(arg)`, line 2) already released unconditionally at line 20 on the success path. When the `if (i)` guard at line 22 is satisfied (i >= 1 tokens, `i` derived from attacker-controlled `arg`) and the realloc at line 23 (size `sizeof *result * (i + 1)`, also derived from the token count) fails, the guard at line 24 admits the failure and lines 25-29 run unconditionally, so this `free(copy)` at line 29 frees the same pointer a second time. No check in the shown code prevents the re-free; the residual range of the token count is unbounded, and the trigger (realloc failure) scales with attacker-chosen input size.

assumptions: `dupstr` returns a fresh, null-terminated heap copy of the input string, so `strtok` at line 6 operates on a valid buffer and terminates (termination does not require any caller invariant).
Pointer-size examples use 8 bytes only for illustration; the double-free is independent of pointer size.
limitations: If `dupstr(arg)` (line 2) returned NULL (allocation failure), `strtok(copy, delim)` at line 6 would be called with NULL; the shown code has no NULL check and `dupstr`'s body is not shown.

If the first-iteration `realloc` at line 7 fails, the guard `!tmp && result` at line 8 excludes the `result == NULL` case, so `result = tmp; result[i++] = dupstr(cptr)` at lines 16-17 writes through NULL; this requires an 8-byte allocation to fail and is not attacker-scalable, so it is not reported as a finding.
`dupstr(cptr)` at line 17 is unchecked; a failing call would store a NULL token in the returned array, whose impact depends on out-of-scope caller dereference behavior.
Integer overflow of `sizeof *result * (i + 1)` at lines 7/23 would require roughly 2^31 tokens (approximately 2GB+ of input); no concrete capacity or bound is identifiable in the shown code.
`strtok` uses process-global static state; thread-safety concerns are not attacker-reachable through the shown code and are out of scope.
NULL `arg`/`delim` handling depends on callers and on `dupstr`'s (unshown) NULL tolerance; the shown code itself imposes no such invariant.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. All memory-safety candidates (NULL store at L71, load_images with NULL dirptr at L74) are gated on allocator failure that no value in the shown types can deterministically trigger, and the remaining dangerous-looking sites (IMF array indexing, destroy(NULL), outfile formatting) depend on macro/callee values not visible in the shown code. Directory-branch failures also set ret=0 (success status), a logic flaw without a demonstrated security mechanism.

assumptions: OPJ_PATH_LEN is OpenJPEG's 4096 constant; wrap math for i*OPJ_PATH_LEN at L71 requires a >=4GB successful allocation, and wrapped offsets still land inside the allocated object.
OPJ_IMF_MAINLEVEL_MAX is 11 in standard OpenJPEG, matching the 12-element limitMSamplesSec array (indices 0..11); the guard at L224 then stays in-bounds including the boundary index 11.
get_num_images (L60) returns the current directory entry count; num_images is not otherwise constrained by the shown code, so its residual range is 0..UINT_MAX.
OpenJPEG cleanup APIs (opj_stream_destroy/opj_destroy_codec/opj_image_destroy) NULL-check their arguments; this is a callee contract not visible in the shown code.
parse_cmdline_encoder never reassigns parameters.cod_format after L51-53, so l_stream at L273 is NULL (not dangling) when reachable, because cod_format is constant across loop iterations.
limitations: L71 `dirptr->filename[i] = ...` has no NULL check for `dirptr->filename` (only `filename_buf` is checked at L66); a NULL store would be CWE-476, but it requires the smaller calloc at L65 to fail after the larger one at L63 succeeded (partial OOM). The deterministic overflow->NULL path is pre-empted because the larger allocation overflows first and exits at L66; no value in the admitted range triggers it, so it is unconfirmed.

L74 `load_images(dirptr, ...)` can receive dirptr==NULL if the fixed-size malloc at L61 fails; attacker does not control that allocation's size and the dereference is inside an unshown callee - OOM-gated only.

Error-status inversion: directory-branch failures set ret=0 at L67-68, L75-76 and L80-81 (and `load_images==1` is treated as failure), while other failure paths and the normal exit at L397 use ret=1/ret=0 consistently; main returns success after failure at L421. CWE-754-class logic flaw with no demonstrated security mechanism.
IMF array: limitMSamplesSec[mainlevel] at L248/L252 is in-bounds only if OPJ_IMF_MAINLEVEL_MAX <= 11; the macro value is not shown, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable rather than a finding.
L273 opj_stream_destroy(l_stream) runs with a NULL l_stream (first iteration/previous iterations destroyed it at L381); safety depends on the unshown callee's NULL handling.
L326/L373/L379 use parameters.outfile (possibly NULL if the unshown parser permits it) in opj_stream_create_default_file_stream, remove(), and fprintf("%s") - caller guarantee not visible.
Directory TOCTOU between get_num_images (L60) and load_images (L74) could overflow filename_buf only if load_images ignores num_images; its body is not shown, so unconfirmable.

The bUseTiles branches (L282-288, L337-356) are unreachable because bUseTiles is initialized OPJ_FALSE at L21 and never assigned; opj_write_tile buffer sizing (l_data_size=512*512*3 for 4 tiles) is therefore not analyzed as reachable.
Chained bSuccess at L333/L358/L363 continues encoding after opj_start_compress failure; final cleanup at L368-376 still returns failure - robustness only.
L347-348 prints unsigned int i with %d in the unreachable tile-error path; type mismatch with no practical impact.
Helpers (parse_cmdline_encoder, get_num_images, load_images, get_next_file, image decoders, opj_* encoder library) are not shown; vulnerabilities inside them are out of scope for this analysis.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The legacy-tag merge is guarded before the headerPut sink by an exact type-equality check (line 16), a count bound admitting [1, 16777216] (line 18), and a fixed-count check (line 20); every mismatch path breaks and returns a non-zero xl->stag (fail-closed). The remaining concerns depend on library internals or capacities not identifiable in the shown code.

assumptions: xlateTags is a statically defined, null-sentinel-terminated table, so the loop at line 7 terminates and never runs past the array; this invariant is not established inside the shown code.
headerGet success implies td.data points to a data region sized consistently with td.count and td.type (library contract); the source blob capacity is not identifiable from the shown code.
rpmtdFreeData resets td so the final call at line 27 is safe on the inner-success path and frees exactly once on all break paths.
rpmTagGetName returns a non-NULL name for every tag present in the static xlateTags table, making the %s argument at line 31 valid.
taglate_s.count is an element count with 0 meaning 'no fixed count requirement'.
rpm_count_t is a signed 32-bit type, so 16*1024*1024=16777216 fits and no comparison overflow occurs in the shown code.
limitations: An out-of-bounds read inside headerGet/headerPut from a crafted sigh tag-data blob cannot be confirmed: the capacity of sigh's data region is not identifiable from the shown code, and the shown guards already bound type and count at lines 16/18/20.
A NULL passed to %s at line 31 would require rpmTagGetName to return NULL for a tag chosen from the static table; that return behavior is not visible in the shown code.
The discarded rasprintf return at line 30 (OOM) has no attacker-controlled volume and its downstream use of *msg is outside the shown code.
Resource usage is bounded by the explicit cap at line 18 (up to ~128 MiB per merged legacy tag); this is a chosen limit rather than unbounded attacker-scaled consumption.
Security impact of successfully merged content depends on downstream consumers of h (signature verification logic), which is not part of the shown code.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() performs no bounds validation on the col parameter before deriving p + col and passing it to mb_head_off(); when has_mbyte is set and col exceeds the current line length by at least two bytes, the helper's backward scan reads past the NUL terminator of the line buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: col is an internal-helper parameter whose residual range is unconstrained by the shown code (stored unvalidated at line 10, used unchanged at line 17). The only guard before this sink is has_mbyte (line 11), which constrains nothing about col's magnitude. With has_mbyte != 0 and a current line of byte length len, any col >= len + 2 makes p + col point past the NUL-terminated buffer (guaranteed capacity len + 1, indices 0..len); mb_head_off's scan then reads at least the byte p + col - 1 >= p + len + 1, one or more bytes beyond capacity — an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) that executes before the unrelated w_wcol guard at line 20.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed 32-bit integer (Vim's standard type); all arithmetic in the shown code stays in that type.
ml_get_curline() returns the current line as a NUL-terminated C string, making its guaranteed readable extent len + 1 bytes, with the NUL at index len.

mb_head_off() scans backward from its second argument, stops at its first argument (base), and returns 0 when its second argument is at or before base — this low-side behavior is assumed as standard callee semantics.
limitations: The trigger for the line-17 over-read requires a caller to supply col larger than the line length; no attacker-controlled call path into display_dollar() is visible in the shown code, so reachability beyond the function boundary is not demonstrated.
The concrete witness depends on the runtime line length (e.g., len = 2, col = 4), so the value is established as a range rather than a fully static value; confidence is accordingly capped at 0.6.

A potential out-of-bounds screen-cell write via edit_putchar() (line 22) when w_wcol is negative or otherwise out of range is not confirmable: curs_columns()'s derivation of w_wcol and the screen buffer capacity are not visible in the shown code, and the guard at line 20 only excludes w_wcol >= w_width.

No integer overflow/underflow was confirmed: on every analyzed path head_off <= col and the line-17 subtraction stays within int range and does not reach an allocation, index, or pointer-arithmetic sink.
No loops exist in the shown code; the backward scan inside mb_head_off() is bounded and terminating by its standard semantics.

verdict.summary: In truemotion1_decode_init, the allocation size passed to av_fast_malloc is computed as s->avctx->width * sizeof(unsigned int) with no validation of width. On 32-bit builds (32-bit size_t), an attacker-controlled width of 0x40000001 wraps the product to 4, allocating a 4-byte vert_pred buffer instead of the required width*4 bytes; the decoder's later width-indexed use of this buffer causes a heap overflow. The wrap is the root cause at the allocation-size sink (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: width is an unconstrained int (no check in the shown code, external container data) flowing directly into the size argument of av_fast_malloc. With width = 0x40000001 on a 32-bit build, (size_t)width * 4 = 0x100000004 mod 2^32 = 4, so the allocation sink receives 4 bytes instead of the required 4,294,967,300 bytes; the L11 NULL guard admits this (allocation succeeds) and init returns success, leaving a grossly undersized buffer for width-indexed decoding. This is CWE-190 at the allocation-size sink.

assumptions: sizeof(unsigned int) == 4 on the analyzed target.
The analysis covers a 32-bit size_t (ILP32) build where the multiplication wraps mod 2^32.
width is attacker-influenced container/bitstream data; the shown code imposes no constraint on it.
priv_data is zero-initialized by the framework, so vert_pred/vert_pred_size are not uninitialized at L10.
limitations: On 64-bit builds no wrap is possible for any int width; the only effect is a huge allocation that fails and is handled by the ENOMEM return at L12.
The resulting heap out-of-bounds write occurs in decoder code not shown here, so CWE-122/CWE-787 cannot be confirmed within the shown code.
The uninitialized read of s->vert_pred/s->vert_pred_size at L10 would only matter if the framework failed to zero priv_data, an invariant not visible in the shown code.
Negative width produces a huge (not small) size and is caught by the existing NULL check, so it is not a demonstrated exploit path.

verdict.summary: The secret file is created world-readable: umask(0022) at line 25 masks only group/other write bits, so ofstream's default 0666 creation mode at line 28 yields 0644 (owner rw, group r, other r). The function's stated contract 'accessible only by the current user' (lines 7-8) is violated, letting any local user read the secret content. Fix by creating the file with mode 0600 (e.g., umask 0077 or open(..., 0600) plus fchmod).

evidence.snippet: mode_t oldUmask = umask(0022); // Owner and group can read and write; others have no permissions
evidence.reason: Permission-policy sink: the constant 0022 masks only group-write (0020) and other-write (0002) bits; group-read (0040) and other-read (0004) remain admitted. Combined with ofstream's default 0666 creation mode, any satisfying of the guards at lines 52 and 16 (argc==4, non-empty argv[1..3]) reaches this call, and no subsequent chmod/fchmod exists (lines 36-45 only write/close). Resulting mode is 0644, so the secret file is world-readable - CWE-732.

File-creation sink executed with umask 0022 (line 25) in effect: a new file is created with mode 0666 & ~0022 = 0644, granting read to group and all other local users, contradicting the 'accessible only by the current user' contract (lines 7-8); an existing file with looser mode is truncated without tightening. CWE-732 mechanism: insecure permissions assigned to a security-critical resource.

assumptions: std::ofstream creates new files using the POSIX default mode 0666 subject to the process umask (libstdc++/glibc behavior), so 0666 & ~0022 = 0644.
The process is effectively single-threaded in the shown code, so the temporary process-global umask change is not a cross-thread hazard here.

argv[1..3] are attacker-controlled when the binary is invoked with untrusted command-line arguments (e.g., by another service or a privileged wrapper); within a plain interactive CLI they are the invoking user's own choice.
limitations: Path traversal / arbitrary file truncation and symlink following via unvalidated directory/filename (lines 22, 28) are not confirmed as standalone findings: the function's documented purpose writes to the caller-supplied directory, and no elevated-privilege context, intended-directory allowlist, or cross-user boundary is visible in the shown code; they would become findings only under an assumed privileged-invocation contract (CWE-22/CWE-59).
main() returns 0 even when saveSecreteFile failed internally (line 59) and file.close() status is discarded (line 44): an error/status-handling weakness with no demonstrated security impact.
If the target file already exists with permissive mode, ofstream does not tighten it; this is part of the CWE-732 mechanism, not a separate bug.
No fixed-size buffers are used (paths are unbounded std::string), so no out-of-bounds memory-safety candidate exists.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response reads in[0] through in[4] at lines 16, 20, 24 and 28 before validating inlen; the length guard at line 37 executes too late. An attacker-controlled token response with inlen < 5 triggers an out-of-bounds read of up to 5 bytes (index == capacity), e.g. inlen == 0 makes in[0] at line 16 read one byte past the buffer.

evidence.reason: Entry-point input inlen has residual range 0..SIZE_MAX with no constraint before this read; inlen is the identifiable capacity of in (used as such at line 37). Witness inlen == 0: index 0 == capacity 0, so in[0] is a 1-byte OOB read (CWE-125). The line-37 guard is unreachable before this sink.

Reads in[2] and in[1] with no length check; requires inlen >= 3 but residual range includes 0..2. Witness inlen == 1: in[1] (index 1 == capacity 1) and in[2] (index 2 > capacity 1) are OOB reads (CWE-125).
Reads in[3] (and in[1]) with no length check; requires inlen >= 4. Witness inlen == 3 with in[2] = 0x00 (branch 1 false, no guard violated): in[3] at index 3 == capacity 3 is an OOB read (CWE-125).

Reads in[4] (and in[1]) with no length check; requires inlen >= 5. Witness inlen == 4 with in[2] = 0x00 and in[3] = 0x00 (branches 1-2 false, no guard violated) and in[1] = 0x82: in[4] at index 4 == capacity 4 is an OOB read (CWE-125).

assumptions: Line 2 is the effective function signature (line 1 is a duplicated prototype); inlen is the size of the in buffer, which line 37 confirms by using inlen as the bound for in.
plaintext has capacity 4096 bytes per its declaration (line 7), and iv has capacity 16 bytes (line 6).
card->drv_data is non-NULL for all paths reaching the parse logic, per the line 10-11 check.
limitations: memcpy(out, plaintext, cipher_len - 2) at line 53 copies up to 4094 bytes into out, but out's capacity is not identifiable from the shown code (caller contract unknown); an OOB write there is unconfirmable.
NULL in, out, out_len, or card is not producible by the shown code's own control flow; NULL dereference would require an out-of-scope caller.

Return values of aes128_decrypt_cbc (line 42) and des3_decrypt_cbc (line 44) are discarded, but their failure semantics are not visible in the shown code, so a confirmed success-after-failure flaw cannot be anchored.

The unpadding loop at line 47 reads plaintext[cipher_len - 2] before checking (cipher_len - 2 > 0), but it is provably in-bounds: line 37 guarantees cipher_len >= 2 (index never negative, loop stops at 2) and max index is 4094 < 4096.
No weak-crypto finding: the AES/3DES algorithm selection (lines 41-44) is driven by token configuration (exdata->smtype), not by attacker-controlled data in this function.
The OOB reads are bounded (up to 5 bytes) and only reachable when a token supplies a short response; impact is DoS/minor information exposure, hence low severity.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, attacker-reachable vulnerability. With BUF_SIZE fixed at 1024 by the only shown caller (main, line 44), read (line 21) returns 0..1010 bytes on success (count<0 handled at line 22, and read cannot exceed its count argument), the ternary at line 29 clamps the NUL-terminator index to [14,1023], so buf is always NUL-terminated in-bounds and strcpy (line 30) copies at most 1024 bytes into the 1024-byte out. No injection, crypto, authz, or error-status flaw is present in the shown code.

assumptions: POSIX read(2) returns between 0 and its count argument on success and -1 on error, so after the count<0 guard (line 22) the success-path count satisfies 0 <= count <= remaining = BUF_SIZE - 14.
The shown caller (line 62) passes BUF_SIZE = 1024 (line 44), and the arrays buf and out (lines 45, 47) each have exactly 1024 elements.
open(2) returns a valid non-negative fd on success (checked at line 13).
limitations: If copy_file_content were invoked with BUF_SIZE < 14, remaining (line 20) would be negative and buf + 14 (line 21) would form a pointer beyond the object (UB on pointer formation); on Linux read would then fail with EINVAL before any memory access, and the path is unreachable because the only shown caller passes 1024. No CWE assigned.
The fd opened at line 12 is not closed on the success path (fd leak); in the shown single-shot entrypoint this does not compound with attacker-controlled volume, so it is not reported as a finding.

When count == remaining (line 21), the NUL placed at BUF_SIZE-1 (line 29) overwrites the final byte read from the file, silently truncating the output by one byte; this is a correctness-only issue with no security impact.

open() on the attacker-supplied filename is the program's intended behavior; no privilege boundary or trusted-directory context is shown in this code, so path/symlink hardening would only matter if the caller changed privilege context.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code. The only candidate is an out-of-bounds segment-register index passed to gen_helper_store_sr(cpu_env, t0, ...) at line 12, but (a) the SR()/rS() extraction masks and (b) the capacities of the env->sr and cpu_gpr arrays are all defined outside the shown code, so no out-of-domain witness value can be derived using the shown code's own types; per the confirmation standard this is a limitation, not a finding. The privilege gate at line 7 is present, admits only pr==0, and correctly blocks user-mode execution by raising a priv-reg exception and returning.

assumptions: ctx->opcode is the 32-bit instruction word being translated and is the only source of the decoded SR()/rS() fields.
The fall-through body (lines 6-13) is compiled only when CONFIG_USER_ONLY is not defined; otherwise only line 4 executes.
t0 is live only from line 11 to line 13, and line 13 executes on every non-exception fall-through path, so the temp allocation is balanced.
limitations: Potential OOB write (CWE-787) at line 12: if SR(ctx->opcode) extracts a field wider than the 4-bit SR field (e.g., bits 16-20 with a 0x1F mask, admitting 16-31) and the segment-register bank env->sr has 16 entries, t0 is forwarded as an out-of-domain index into a name-implied index sink. Unconfirmed because neither the SR() macro body nor the env->sr capacity is present in the shown code, so no witness satisfying 't0 >= capacity' is expressible with the shown code's own types.
Potential OOB read at line 12 via cpu_gpr[rS(ctx->opcode)]: rS() width and the cpu_gpr array size are not identifiable from the shown code, so no boundary claim can be confirmed.

The safety of the call cannot be established from an unshown bounds check inside gen_helper_store_sr; the not-vulnerable verdict rests on the candidate failing the confirmation standard, not on any in-scope protective index bound (the only in-scope guard, line 7, gates privilege, not value).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The page-array index at line 20 is strictly capped by the break at lines 17-19 (page_idx < page_count admits only 0..page_count-1), the 8-byte file read into tmp[] is validated by the != 8 status check at lines 29-32 before r_read_le64 at line 34, the chain walk cannot stall or loop unboundedly because delta == 0 breaks at lines 216-218 and delta >= 1 advances cursor by >= 4 bytes, segment indices are capped by nsegs/segs_count at line 3, every pointer_format switch arm assigns delta/stride with a returning default at lines 145-147, and callback status is honored at lines 212-213. Remaining concerns (actual allocation sizes of page_start/segs/chained_starts, fileoff+filesize wrap feeding the guarded page loop, and limit_end-8 underflow for limit_end < 8) depend on loader invariants or caller ranges absent from the shown code and are listed as limitations.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at is bounds-checked on bin->b and returns the actual number of bytes read, so a short/EOF read is detected by the != 8 test at line 29.

bin->segs is allocated with at least segs_count entries, bin->chained_starts with at least nsegs entries, and page_start with at least page_count entries by the Mach-O loader; these capacities are not established in the shown code.
The dyld chained-pointer bitfields (next, ordinal, addend, target, etc.) are unsigned, so delta extracted from raw_ptr is non-negative and delta*stride cannot overflow ut64 (max ~2^22).
limitations: An OOB read of page_start[page_idx] would require page_start to be allocated smaller than page_count, which is a loader invariant not visible in the shown code; the visible guard at lines 17-19 makes index == page_count unreachable.

end = start + filesize at line 12 can wrap, making the line 15 subtraction underflow to a huge page_end_idx; the impact is capped by the page_count break at lines 17-19, so no in-range index is produced.

cursor arithmetic at lines 24 and 216 can wrap when start is near 2^64, but the while condition at line 25 re-bounds the walk and the read status check at lines 29-32 prevents any unvalidated read; no memory-safety consequence is derivable in the shown code.
limit_end - 8 at line 149 underflows for limit_end < 8, widening the callback filter for an absurd caller-supplied range; it has no memory impact in the shown code.
NULL dereference of bin->b, bin->chained_starts[i] (checked at line 4), or a mismatched allocation size depends on state produced outside the shown code.
Per-entry scanning is linear in the on-disk data bounded by end/limit_end and by reads failing past EOF; no attacker-amplified resource-exhaustion loop is derivable.

verdict.summary: The subdomain validity check is permanently disabled by the constant-false guard `if (0)` (line 23), so the attacker-controlled subdomain prefix is embedded into the URL verbatim at line 27. Input such as `@evil.com/` yields `https://@evil.com/.example.com`, which standard URL parsing resolves to host `evil.com`, producing an open-redirect/URL-spoofing primitive despite the trusted-domain contract.

evidence.reason: argv[2] (entry-point input, unbounded length, all characters admitted by the shown code) flows via subdomain_prefix into the %s argument here with no escaping or filtering. The only reachable guard, `subdomain_prefix.length() > 0` (line 26), admits any non-empty string; the validation branch promised on line 22 is dead because `if (0)` (line 23) has an empty admitted set. Witness `@evil.com/` passes line 37 (argc==3) and line 26, and line 27 produces `https://@evil.com/.example.com`, whose authority resolves to host `evil.com` under standard URL semantics, demoting the trusted domain `example.com` to the path (CWE-601 open redirect / URL spoofing).

assumptions: The URL string produced by get_url_to_visit is subsequently consumed as a URL (e.g., for redirect or navigation) by a standard parser following RFC 3986 authority semantics.
limitations: Unchecked snprintf return values (lines 24, 27, 29): long inputs are silently truncated to 255 chars. snprintf is size-bounded, so there is no memory-safety impact, and truncation preserves any injected prefix, so it is not an independent root cause (likely CWE-754-style hardening concern only).
If the URL is only printed to stdout (line 47) and never used to navigate or redirect, the demonstrated impact is limited to spoofing of displayed content.
domain itself is taken from argv[1] without validation despite the 'trusted' comment, which widens the attack surface but is not the primary finding.
The static url buffer (line 20) is non-reentrant; the shown single-threaded main calls the function once, so no confirmed impact.
Newline/control characters in the subdomain could reach stdout (line 47), but the shown code provides no security-sensitive logging boundary, so log injection is not confirmed.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is demonstrable within the shown code. The teardown loops index h_event_start_decoding and h_decoding_thread with i < allocated_decoding_thread_count, but the arrays' capacity and the number of initialized elements are established by an unshown thread-creation path, so all OOB index claims are unconfirmable. Discarded returns from sem_post/pthread_join/sem_destroy and a possible mismatch between the loop bound and the actually created/initialized thread state are recorded as limitations rather than findings.

assumptions: pbi is a valid, non-NULL VP8D_COMP pointer established by the caller.

The unshown thread-creation path initialized h_event_start_decoding/h_decoding_thread such that allocated_decoding_thread_count equals the number of valid elements, and h_event_end_decoding was initialized before this function can run.
vpx_free(NULL) is safe and POSIX semantics of sem_post/pthread_join/sem_destroy apply.
limitations: OOB sem_post/pthread_join/sem_destroy at lines 10, 11, and 15 if allocated_decoding_thread_count exceeds the capacity of h_event_start_decoding/h_decoding_thread: the arrays' capacity is not identifiable from the shown code (no declaration, allocation, or named constant), so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.

Discarded return values of sem_post (line 10), pthread_join (line 11), and sem_destroy (lines 15 and 18): a failing call requires an invalid/uninitialized semaphore or thread handle, a state no value of the fields in the shown code can produce; this is an unchecked-status robustness concern, not a demonstrated status-handling flaw.

Possible NULL or invalid dereference at lines 10, 11, 15, and 18 if the semaphore/thread fields are NULL or uninitialized while b_multithreaded_rd is nonzero: that state is produced outside the shown code and cannot be demonstrated here.

A teardown race (destroying semaphores while a live worker still uses them, or freeing structures mid-decode) would require the loop bound to overstate the number of threads actually created/initialized, which depends on the unshown creation code.

verdict.summary: saveSecreteFile builds the destination path from unvalidated entry-point strings (argv[1], argv[2]) and opens it with std::ofstream(out|trunc) without O_NOFOLLOW, O_EXCL, or any lstat/ownership/mode check. A pre-placed symlink at the destination is followed by the open, so the subsequent write truncates/overwrites an arbitrary file and the umask(0077)-based 600-only confidentiality guarantee is defeated because the target inode is not newly created.

evidence.reason: filepath (line 23) is derived entirely from entry-point inputs directory/filename (argv[1]/argv[2], line 58); the only guard on the path, the non-empty check at line 17, admits every non-empty string, so a filename naming an existing symlink (e.g., "victim" where /tmp/victim -> /home/u/.bashrc) passes. ofstream uses standard open() semantics that follow symlinks, so O_TRUNC truncates the symlink target and umask(0077) at line 26 cannot help because no new inode with 0600 is created — arbitrary-file truncation as the running user (primary CWE-59).

content is untrusted entry-point input (argv[3]) admitted by line 17's non-empty check and is written into whichever object line 29 opened; when that object is the followed symlink target, the secret is stored at the attacker-chosen location with the target's existing permissions, breaking the documented only-current-user confidentiality requirement. No guard on the resolved path exists between lines 23 and 37.

assumptions: argv strings are NUL-terminated C strings, so the std::string values cannot contain embedded NULs.
std::ofstream uses the default exception mask, so open/write failures surface through is_open() and fail() rather than exceptions.
umask() is process-global; the shown program is single-threaded.
limitations: CWE-22 path traversal is not confirmed: directory and filename are both entry-point inputs and no trusted base directory is established in the shown code, so '../' in filename grants no additional boundary escape.

CWE-732 (a pre-existing world-readable destination keeps mode 0644 under O_TRUNC because umask only applies at inode creation) shares the same root cause at the same open sink and is folded into the CWE-59 finding rather than reported as an independent CWE.
Process-wide umask race (CWE-362) requires concurrent threads, which the shown code does not create.
No memory-safety, injection, crypto, or integer-wraparound sinks are present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header stores av_malloc results for smk->frm_size and smk->frm_flags without NULL checks (lines 36-37), then writes through them in loops driven by the file-supplied frame count. The line 32 guard admits frames up to 0xFFFFFF, so an attacker can force allocations of up to 67,108,860 and 16,777,215 bytes; when either allocation fails, the loop store at line 41 or 44 dereferences NULL, crashing the parser on untrusted media (CWE-476, DoS).

evidence.reason: Taint: smk->frames is an entry-point file value (get_le32 at line 14) whose residual range after the line 32 guard (frames > 0xFFFFFF rejected) is [0, 0xFFFFFF]. Sink: frm_size was set from av_malloc(frames*4) at line 36 with no NULL check; witness frames = 0xFFFFFF is in the guard's admitted set and requests 67,108,860 bytes. When av_malloc fails, loop 40-41 executes (i=0 < frames) and stores 4 bytes through NULL at i=0 — an unconditional NULL-pointer write (CWE-476). The admitted set does not exclude the failing allocation, and no NULL test exists between line 36 and this store.

Taint: same smk->frames entry-point value, admitted [0, 0xFFFFFF] by the line 32 guard. Sink: frm_flags was set from av_malloc(frames) at line 37 with no NULL check; witness frames = 0xFFFFFF is admitted and requests 16,777,215 bytes. If that allocation fails, loop 43-44 executes (i=0 < frames) and stores 1 byte through NULL at i=0 — an unconditional NULL-pointer write (CWE-476). The guard's admitted set intersects the failing-allocation state, and no NULL test precedes this store.

assumptions: SmackerContext::frames and ::treesize are 32-bit unsigned (inferred from assignment of get_le32()/get_byte() ByteIO returns and the UINT_MAX/4 comparison); the struct definition is not part of the shown code.
av_malloc() returns NULL on allocation failure; get_le32()/get_byte() return 0 past end-of-file and get_buffer' returns a short count at EOF (standard ByteIO/avutil semantics).
st->codec->extradata_size is int-sized, so treesize+16 <= 1,073,741,838 fits without overflow.
limitations: Whether av_malloc(67,108,860)/av_malloc(16,777,215) actually fails depends on allocator/system state; on typical 64-bit hosts with lazy commit the NULL deref may not trigger, capping confidence at 0.6.

smk->pts_inc negation/multiplication (lines 58-61) can invoke signed-overflow UB (e.g., INT32_MIN negation or *100 wrap), but the corrupted value only reaches av_reduce/av_set_pts_info (time base) and never an allocation-size, index, length, or pointer sink, so it is not a confirmed CWE-190 finding.

ast[i]->index dereference (line 70) after unchecked av_new_stream is also a NULL deref in principle, but it involves at most 7 fixed-size small allocations with no attacker-controlled size, so it falls under the unchecked-allocation limitation rather than a confirmed finding.
Error paths at lines 47-49 and 92-96 leak frm_size/frm_flags/extradata; these are single-shot leaks without attacker-controlled compounding volume and are out of scope.

The up-to-~1 GiB extradata allocation (line 83) is NULL-checked (lines 85-89) and fails gracefully; it is a single allocation with no compounding loop, so it is not a confirmed resource-exhaustion finding.

No integer overflow at a memory sink is confirmed: line 32 caps frames so frames*4 <= 0x3FFFFFC (no wrap) and keeps loop indices in-bounds when allocations succeed; line 20 caps treesize so treesize+16 fits int.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code. The dangerous-looking allocation av_new_packet(pkt, size + DXA_EXTRA_SIZE + pal_size) at line 52 is protected by the explicit guard at line 48 (size > 0xFFFFFF returns AVERROR_INVALIDDATA), which bounds size to [0, 16777215]; the maximum sum (16777215 + 8 + 772 = 16777995) cannot wrap uint32, and every subsequent copy/read (lines 54, 55, 60) stays exactly within the allocated packet. The remaining concerns are unconfirmable from the shown code: AV_RB32(buf + 5) at line 47 reads bytes 5..8 of an 8-element buf only if DXA_EXTRA_SIZE <= 8 (constant value not shown), and discarding the avio_read return at line 40 can leave uninitialized stack bytes in pal that reach output packets only if a short read occurs without setting EOF, which buffered-file semantics in the shown loop (line 21) exclude.

assumptions: DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is a positive compile-time constant (the shown code requires >= 4 for the line 43 read length); its numeric value is not visible in the shown code.
avio_read/av_get_packet/av_new_packet follow standard AVIO/AVPacket semantics: full byte counts on success, negative values on I/O error, and short reads on a buffered file imply EOF is recorded.
DXAContext fields (bytes_left, bpc, frames, vidpos, wavpos, has_sound, readvid) are set by header parsing outside the shown code and are treated as internal-helper state here.
url_feof at the loop top reflects the EOF state of the AVIO layer, so a short palette read from a finite file terminates the while loop before a subsequent chunk tag can be consumed.
limitations: AV_RB32(buf + 5) at line 47 performs a 4-byte load spanning buf[5..8]; since the numeric value of DXA_EXTRA_SIZE (buf's declared capacity at line 6) is not shown, the out-of-bounds boundary is unconfirmable. If DXA_EXTRA_SIZE == 8 (the historical FFmpeg value), this is a 1-byte stack out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose only effect is the low byte of size, still capped by line 48; if DXA_EXTRA_SIZE >= 9 it is in-bounds.

The discarded return of avio_read(s->pb, pal + 4, 768) at line 40 is an error/status-handling flaw (CWE-754 pattern): on a short read, pal_size is still set to 772 (line 38) and pal[4+r..771] retain uninitialized stack bytes that memcpy at lines 31/60 would place into returned packets. Reachability of that copy is not demonstrable inside the shown code for buffered files because EOF terminates the loop at line 21 before a following NULL/FRAM tag can be parsed; a short read without EOF requires framework stream semantics not shown.

The unchecked avio_seek calls at lines 10 and 20 are robustness-only: any failed seek surfaces through subsequent read statuses that are checked (lines 14, 22, 43, 55).

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. verdict.summary: smk->frames is read from the file at line 13 with residual range [0, 0xFFFFFFFF]. assumptions: smk->frames is a uint32_t field: get_le32 returns uint32_t and is assigned without a cast, and line 27's 0xFFFFFF test is used as an upper-bound check.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code alone. assumptions: `colnr_T` is a signed integer type, evidenced by the comparison `col_arg < 0` at line 3; its exact width is irrelevant because only `col >= 0` is subsequently used.
`redrawing()` returning non-zero is the only gate (line 6) for the operations that follow.

limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) at line 18: after the only shown constraint `col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg` (line 3), `col` has residual range [0, COLNR_MAX] with no upper bound. Any `col` larger than the current line's byte length makes `p + col` (line 18) point past the end of the line buffer before `mb_head_off` dereferences it. Not confirmed because the capacity of the object returned by `ml_get_curline()` (line 17) is not identifiable from the shown code, so the exact excess cannot be computed; there is also no protective upper-bound check in the shown code, so real-world safety would depend on an out-of-scope caller invariant that `col_arg` never exceeds the line length.

Potential NULL dereference (CWE-476) at lines 17-18: `p = ml_get_curline()` is not checked before `mb_head_off(p, ...)` is called, but no path inside the shown code can produce a NULL from `ml_get_curline()`, so the NULL dereference is not confirmable.

If the out-of-bounds read at line 18 occurred, the garbage `mb_head_off` result could also drive `curwin->w_cursor.col` outside its normal range (line 18) and feed `curs_columns()` (line 20); this is a downstream symptom of the unconfirmed read, not an independent finding.

Assigning an unbounded `col` into `curwin->w_cursor.col` (line 11) before `curs_columns(FALSE)` (line 20) could propagate invalid window-geometry state, but `curs_columns` is not shown and any impact depends on the unconfirmed OOB candidate.

evidence.reason: argv[1] is an entry-point input whose residual range (no constraint in the shown code) includes the empty string; with argv = {'./a.out', ''} the guard at line 20 (argc >= 2) admits the path, buf2 is allocated with capacity strlen(argv[1]) + 1 = 1 byte at line 26, and len = 0 at line 8. The derived index -1 is out of the object's domain [0..0] by 1 byte and is produced entirely by the shown code's own arithmetic.

assumptions: argv[1] is a valid NUL-terminated string for argc >= 2, per standard C semantics of argv (argv[argc] == NULL); this is consistent with the guard on line 20.
buf2 is the object accessed by trim_spaces at the call site (line 34); its capacity is identifiable from line 26 as strlen(argv[1]) + 1.
limitations: The out-of-bounds write at line 10 (str[-1] = '\0') and any further backward walk require the heap byte preceding buf2 to equal 0x20, which is allocator-layout data not controllable from the shown code; this escalation is not independently confirmed and is not given its own CWE.

malloc returns (lines 25-27) are unchecked; a NULL buf2 would be dereferenced by strcpy at line 29, but this requires OOM on an allocation sized by an argv string, is not attacker-controllable under OS argument-size limits, and has only DoS impact — recorded as a hardening concern, not a finding.
The size_t -> int narrowing at line 8 is implementation-defined only for N > INT_MAX; such argv lengths are unreachable in practice, so the corresponding massive OOB access is speculative.

If trim_spaces were ever called with a string literal it would also write to read-only memory, but the shown call site passes the writable heap buffer buf2, so that path is not reachable within the shown code.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in `args.size() + 1` (line 4) when an attacker-controlled argument array reaches int64 size INT64_MAX: the addition wraps to INT64_MIN, which is converted into the capacity argument of PackedArray::MakeReserve, under-allocating the array that the compact() fills (lines 7-8) then populate with up to args.size()+1 entries, risking a heap out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Entry-point input `args` has unconstrained non-negative int64 size 0..INT64_MAX (no guard bounds it; the only branch, `if (v)` at line 6, is independent of `args.size()`). With args.size() == INT64_MAX the int64 addition wraps to INT64_MIN, and this wrapped value is the size/capacity argument consumed by the reserve/allocation helper at this call site, so the reservation no longer covers the up-to-args.size()+1 stores performed by compact(v, ret, varname) and compact(v, ret, args) at lines 7-8, which is the exact invariant the line-4 expression 'args.size() + 1' encodes. Primary mechanism: CWE-190 integer overflow corrupting an allocation-size argument.

assumptions: Array::size() returns a non-negative int64_t count, so the admitted boundary value is INT64_MAX.
The int64 addition at the overflow boundary wraps (two's-complement behavior of the compilers used for HHVM).
PackedArray::MakeReserve's argument is consumed as a capacity/size, per its name and the shown code's use.
The compact() calls store at most 1 + args.size() entries total (1 from varname, args.size() from args).
limitations: Constructing a real HHVM Array with INT64_MAX (or even >2^32) elements is infeasible in practice due to memory, so the demonstrated witness is a type-domain boundary value and practical exploitation is implausible.
The exact width/signedness of MakeReserve's capacity parameter is not visible in the shown code; the claim relies only on the wrap and the conversion failing to preserve INT64_MAX+1.

Whether the unshown compact()/Array-append path raw-fills past the undersized reserve (OOB heap write, CWE-787) or reallocates/grows safely is not confirmable from the shown code, so no secondary CWE is asserted.
The NULL VarEnv path is guarded by `if (v)` (line 6); skipping the fills and returning the empty array is correct behavior, not a finding.
No loops, format-string sinks, injection sinks, crypto, file handling, or authz logic exist in the shown code to analyze further.

verdict.summary: truemotion1_decode_init derives the heap allocation size from the unvalidated signed int avctx->width (line 10). In width * sizeof(unsigned int), width is converted to size_t and multiplied in unsigned arithmetic; on 32-bit targets a width such as 1073741825 wraps min_size to 4, so av_fast_malloc returns a 4-byte buffer, line 11's non-NULL guard admits it, and init returns success — leaving decode-time vertical-prediction writes to an undersized heap buffer (CWE-190 root cause at the allocation-size sink).

evidence.reason: The allocation-size argument derives from the entry-point input s->avctx->width (int, residual range [-2147483648, 2147483647]; no constraint in the shown code). On a 32-bit size_t target, width = 1073741825 yields (size_t)1073741825 * 4 = 4294967300 mod 2^32 = 4, which is consumed by the allocation sink and produces a non-NULL 4-byte buffer. The only guard on the path, line 11 (if (!s->vert_pred)), admits this non-NULL undersized buffer, so init returns success at line 15; the buffer is ~2^32-4 bytes too small for the codec's width-driven writes, yielding a heap OOB write in decode. Primary CWE-190: unsigned multiplication wrap corrupts the allocation size at the sink.

assumptions: The wrap witness requires a 32-bit size_t target; the expression's type is size_t because sizeof(unsigned int) yields size_t.
av_fast_malloc/av_malloc follow standard semantics: allocate at least min_size, return NULL for sizes above the allocator cap, and store the size only on success.
avctx->width is attacker-influenced container/bitstream metadata because the shown code imposes no constraint on it.
limitations: Negative width yields a huge size_t min_size (e.g., width = -1 -> 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC on 64-bit); av_fast_malloc fails and the line 11 NULL check returns a clean error, so that path has no confirmed impact in the shown code.
On 64-bit size_t the positive-width product cannot wrap (max (2^31-1)*4 = 2^33-4), so the overflow finding is limited to 32-bit builds.

The actual out-of-bounds write enabled by the undersized vert_pred occurs in truemotion1_decode_frame, which is not part of the shown code; it is not independently confirmed, so no CWE-787 is attached.

A width near 536870911 can also cause a successful ~2 GiB allocation on 64-bit; this is a single-shot allocation, not scaled by attacker volume in a reachable loop, so it is not reported as a resource-exhaustion finding.
A width of exactly 2^30 on 32-bit wraps min_size to 0, which makes av_fast_malloc free/set NULL and returns a clean error; only wrapped sizes in (0, cap] reach the success path.

verdict.summary: In web builds (PLATFORM_WEB), SetClipboardText embeds the attacker-influenced `text` parameter verbatim into a JavaScript snippet passed to emscripten_run_script without escaping or filtering (line 7). A single quote in `text` terminates the JS string literal and allows arbitrary script execution in the embedding page. For example, text = "x');alert(1);//" yields navigator.clipboard.writeText('x');alert(1);//') which executes alert(1).

The literal format string wraps it in single quotes and substitutes it raw via %s, so a value such as "x');alert(1);//" — a member of the admitted set of every guard on this path (the only guard is the compile-time PLATFORM_WEB selection) — survives intact to the sink and terminates the JS string literal, closes the writeText call, executes the injected statement, and comments out the trailing characters. emscripten_run_script is an eval-style dynamic-code sink and the generated script string is derived entirely inside the shown code at this line, yielding arbitrary JavaScript execution in the page (CWE-95).

assumptions: Builds define exactly one of PLATFORM_DESKTOP or PLATFORM_WEB, so the web branch is selectable by build configuration.
emscripten_run_script executes its argument as JavaScript with the privileges of the embedding page.
TextFormat implements %s as ordinary argument substitution without escaping (consistent with the literal quotes in the shown format string).
limitations: The desktop branch (line 4, glfwSetClipboardString) shows no confirmed vulnerability from the code provided; a NULL `text` is not producible by any path inside the shown code, and non-UTF-8 content is a contract concern without a confirmed security mechanism here.
TextFormat's internal buffer size is not shown, so any truncation-related boundary claim for very long strings is unconfirmable from this code.
If a caller supplied only developer-controlled static literals, impact would be limited; however, the shown code itself imposes no such constraint on `text`.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response trusts the card-supplied TLV length: in_len up to 65535 (parsed at lines 19-31 with no bound check) is passed as in_len-1 to the AES/3DES decrypt calls, which write into the 4096-byte stack buffer plaintext, causing a stack buffer overflow; additionally, in_len-2 underflows for in_len in {0,1}, producing a deterministic out-of-bounds read in the unpadding loop.

Witness in[1]=0x82,in[4]=0x01,in[2]=0xFF,in[3]=0xFF passes the admitted set of line 27 and yields in_len=65535; length arg in_len-1=65534 exceeds the 4096-byte capacity of plaintext (line 6) by ~61438 bytes and is consumed as the decrypt output length, overflowing the stack buffer (CWE-121). The same sink is reachable with in_len=0 via unsigned underflow in_len-1=SIZE_MAX.

Identical mechanism to the AES call at line 38: the same unguarded in_len-1 (residual [0,65535]) is passed as the decrypt output length into plaintext[4096] (line 6), overflowing the stack buffer for any in_len >= 4098, e.g., in_len=65535 via the admitted branch at line 27 (CWE-121).

For in_len=1 (admitted by line 19 with in[1]=1, in[2]=0x01, in[0]=0x98), in_len-2 underflows unsigned size_t to SIZE_MAX; the left operand plaintext[in_len-2] is evaluated before the (in_len-2 > 0) operand, so the guard does not protect the read, and the underflowed index itself satisfies >0. Index SIZE_MAX on the 4096-byte plaintext (line 6) is an out-of-bounds read by ~SIZE_MAX-4096 (CWE-125).

assumptions: size_t is 64-bit unsigned on the target platform, so in_len-1 and in_len-2 underflow to SIZE_MAX-range values.

NULL from the caller for card/out/out_len (lines 9, 49, 50) is a caller-side precondition, not a path produced in the shown code.

The all-zero CBC IV (line 5) with fixed keys is a design concern but cannot be confirmed as a weakness without key/IV-reuse context not present in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability.
