verdict.summary: Missing error returns after header/position/count validation in rv10_decode_packet let attacker-controlled MB coordinates (s->mb_x/s->mb_y set by the slice-header decode) exceed the picture bounds; the loop then passes out-of-range row/column indices into the MB-decode/write functions, causing out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787). Additionally, after a detected bitstream overrun the loop continues decoding past the 8*buf_size2 bit cap, causing out-of-bounds packet reads (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: s->mb_x/s->mb_y are entry-point input from the slice header with an all-int residual range: the only local checks (L14-L17, L20-L22, L11-L13) merely log and never return. With the concrete witness s->mb_x == s->mb_width, s->mb_y == 1, mb_count == 1 (mb_width>=1, mb_height>=2, current_picture_ptr != NULL), every guard on the path admits the value and the loop body reaches this statement with column index == capacity; the L83 wrap (++s->mb_x == s->mb_width) cannot fire once the coordinate is at/above mb_width, so the index stays out of the [0, mb_width) domain. MPV_decode_mb writes the decoded macroblock into frame buffers indexed by (s->mb_x, s->mb_y): out-of-bounds write, CWE-787.

Same out-of-domain MB coordinate flows to this index consumer before any wrap can occur: with s->mb_x == s->mb_width (admitted by the log-only guards L14-L17/L20-L22), ff_update_block_index computes block offsets from s->mb_x/s->mb_y, dereferencing block arrays at column index >= mb_width on the first loop iteration; CWE-787.

After L70-L74 refuses to extend s->gb.size_in_bits once get_bits_count exceeds 8*buf_size2 (the cap the shown code itself treats as the safe buffer size), L75-L77 only logs the overrun; neither path returns or breaks, so a subsequent loop iteration re-enters this statement with the bitreader positioned beyond the 8*buf_size2 bit capacity of buf, and reads past the packet buffer; also on SLICE_ERROR the MB write at L80 still runs on the failure state. Out-of-bounds read, CWE-125.

assumptions: s->mb_width and s->mb_height are positive after a successful-enough header decode, so [0, mb_width) x [0, mb_height) is the valid MB domain implied by the shown checks (L14) and wrap logic (L83).

For the primary witness with current_picture_ptr == NULL, the L27 coordinate reset does not run because the reset is guarded by if(s->current_picture_ptr) at L24; with a non-NULL picture pointer and a non-(0,0) coordinate, the L23 block is skipped entirely.
8*buf_size2 is treated by the shown code (L70/L72) as the bit capacity of the buffer backing s->gb.
limitations: The failure of MPV_frame_start (L29) is ignored and decoding continues into MB decode; a resulting NULL/invalid-picture dereference is plausible but the failure state is produced inside the callee, so it is not independently confirmed.

With mb_count < 0 (L11 log-only), the loop is skipped but ff_er_add_slice at L92 still receives s->mb_x-1, which can be -1 when s->mb_x == 0; the callee's handling of negative/out-of-domain coordinates is not visible in the shown code, so it is not reported as a finding.
Int overflow in mb_pos/left (L18-L19) and buf_size*8 / 8*buf_size2 (L6, L70-L72) for extreme values is possible in the shown int types but no demonstrated path to a memory sink was confirmed.

The precise byte-level extent of the OOB write/read inside ff_h263_decode_mb / MPV_decode_mb / ff_update_block_index is not visible; the anchors are the out-of-domain indices/sizes the shown code itself derives and forwards.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476) at line 129: encrypted_pass is initialized to NULL (line 28) and assigned from pwd->pw_passwd (line 46) with no NULL check; on builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM (the only NULL-constraining branch, lines 59-64, is compiled out), an unauthenticated RADIUS request naming an account whose passwd entry has pw_passwd == NULL dereferences NULL and crashes the daemon — remote denial of service.

evidence.reason: Sink dereferences encrypted_pass. Phase 1: encrypted_pass is OS/library-derived data whose NULL-ness the shown code never constrains — line 28 sets it to NULL and line 46 assigns pwd->pw_passwd after only the struct (not the field) is NULL-checked at line 43; line 59's own 'encrypted_pass == NULL' clause confirms the author models NULL as admissible. Phase 3: on a build without HAVE_GETSPNAM (#ifdef at line 49 not compiled), the path for an admitted username (line 23 passes, line 43 passes while pw_passwd == NULL, lines 49-65 absent) reaches line 129 with encrypted_pass == NULL and faults. The guard that could remove the NULL only exists inside the HAVE_GETSPNAM branch, so the missing check is precisely the absent NULL test on pw_passwd for non-shadow builds; residual range is sound but the NULL originates in OS passwd data, so no single constant is derivable from the shown code alone. Mechanism: CWE-476 NULL dereference, crash = remote DoS.

assumptions: HAVE_GETSPNAM is a compile-time macro that may be undefined for the analyzed build, exposing the pw_passwd path (lines 43-46) without the NULL guard in lines 59-64.
request->username is a framework-validated User-Name attribute; only its non-NULL status is guarded inside the shown code (lines 23-25), and vp_strvalue is assumed NUL-terminated by the framework.
pairmove is assumed to follow standard move semantics (source pointer nulled), making pairfree(&vp) at line 136 operate on NULL.
request->timestamp is framework-provided seconds-since-epoch; the division at line 107 and comparisons at lines 106-107 / 117-118 stay within the declared types.
limitations: The NULL value of pwd->pw_passwd originates in OS passwd data, not attacker input; on glibc the field is never NULL, so exposure is limited to non-glibc builds or builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM — hence confidence 0.6 and medium severity.

Confirmed but lower-severity log injection (CWE-117): entry-point name (and pwd->pw_shell) flow unescaped into radlog/radlog_request %s arguments at lines 39, 77, 95-96, 108, 119, so embedded CR/LF can forge log lines; not reported as the primary finding.

If the framework ever stored a non-string attribute under User-Name, request->username->vp_strvalue could be NULL and getpwnam(name) at line 43 would fault; that invariant is not visible in the shown code.
A double-free/use-after-free at lines 135-136 would require pairmove to leave vp non-NULL; with standard move semantics the pattern is safe, and the callee body is not shown.
No OOB read is confirmable: all strlen/strcmp uses rely on NUL-terminated OS strings, and the getusershell loop (lines 87-92) is bounded by file contents and terminates for every input.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only dangerous-looking construct — `goto error` with uninitialized `rc` (lines 9/2) — is structurally safe because the sole consumer of `rc` (line 30) is positioned before the `error:` label (line 32), making an uninitialized read unreachable; every switch arm assigns `rc` (lines 14, 18, 23, 28), and the shown code contains no loop, buffer, index arithmetic, injection, crypto, or file/authz sink. `packet` is forwarded opaquely with no derived size/index.

Only `rc == SSH_ERROR` is checked (line 30); a hypothetical other failure code from a helper being treated as success is unconfirmable from the shown code.
NULL `session` or `session->next_crypto` is not producible from any path in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable in the shown code. The potentially dangerous operations are provably bounded: the post-'>' scan (L16) reads only up to the string's terminating NUL because the L13 guard admits k in [1, L-1]; the memmove route-strip (L26) copies at most strlen(user) bytes within the NUL-terminated user string with defined overlap; the domain copy (L41) is a bounded strlcpy from a framework-provided source. All candidates that could not be fully confirmed (NULL args, helper-internal parsing, unknown buffer capacities, empty-path acceptance after route-stripping) are recorded in limitations.

After text_to_mailaddr returns success (L20-21), maddr->user and maddr->domain are NUL-terminated, in-bounds C strings, as consumed at L23-L42.

memmove overlap semantics (ISO C) make the L26 copy well-defined.

Capacities of line, maddr->user, and maddr->domain (struct mailaddr layout) are not identifiable from the shown code, so no boundary/OOB claim against those buffers is confirmable.
A NULL args at L18 would be a NULL-deref, but NULL cannot be produced by any path inside the shown code.

If text_to_mailaddr stores 'a:' in maddr->user, the route-strip (L23-27) collapses it to empty so L32 accepts MAIL FROM:<a:> as the empty return path (and <a:b@c> normalizes to <b@c>); this depends on the unshown helper and bypasses no security mechanism with demonstrated impact beyond input-validation laxity.
A non-NUL-terminated line would over-read at strchr (L12) already; that is a caller-contract violation, out of scope.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code: qemu_register_machine contains only a struct initialization, one g_strconcat call, one type_register call, and a constant return 0. There are no branches or loops, no arithmetic or indexing, and no injection, crypto, file, or authz sinks. The only suspicious operations (unchecked use of m->name, leaked concatenated name, discarded type_register status) each depend on out-of-scope caller contracts or single-shot, non-compounding effects and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

assumptions: TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX is a compile-time constant string; the explicit NULL at line 4 terminates g_strconcat's varargs.
g_strconcat has standard GLib semantics: it allocates exactly the concatenation length, yields a NUL-terminated result, and aborts on allocation failure rather than returning NULL.
type_register is void in QEMU usage, and even under its name-implied registration semantics no failure-dependent statement follows it in the shown code.
limitations: A NULL m or NULL m->name supplied by an out-of-scope caller would be dereferenced by g_strconcat at line 4 (CWE-476); the NULL is not producible inside the shown code, so the claim is unconfirmed.
If m->name were not NUL-terminated, g_strconcat at line 4 could over-read; the string's capacity/termination invariant is not identifiable from the shown code, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable.
The string allocated by g_strconcat and stored in ti.name (line 4) is never freed; this is a single-shot leak with no attacker-controlled volume in the shown code, so it is not reported as a finding.
The return status of type_register (line 9) is discarded, but no failure path or subsequent failure-dependent operation exists in the shown code, so no CWE-390/754 claim is confirmed.

verdict.summary: When sps->chroma_format_idc is 0, the only shown write to pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom (line 12) is skipped, yet lines 17 and 22 unconditionally read the field and feed the indeterminate value into av_log and into the shift computing chroma_def, which is undefined behavior for counts outside [0,31] and corrupts the default chroma weights otherwise.

evidence.reason: Read-before-init (CWE-457): pwt is an internal-helper parameter whose pre-call contents are unconstrained by the shown code. The witness sps->chroma_format_idc == 0 is a member of line 11's excluded set and is admitted by the shown code, so line 12 (the only shown write to chroma_log2_weight_denom) is skipped, but line 17 still reads the field unconditionally; no guard on this path initializes it.

The indeterminate value from the line 12-skipped path reaches a signed left shift: a count outside [0,31] is undefined behavior, and any value outside [0,7] sets chroma_def incorrectly; that value is then stored as default chroma weights at lines 63-64 and copied at lines 73-74. The clamp at lines 17-20 cannot sanitize an indeterminate value. Primary mechanism: use of uninitialized memory (CWE-457).

assumptions: get_ue_golomb/get_se_golomb/get_bits1 behave as FFmpeg bit-reader helpers (unsigned/signed/0-1 returns); their overread behavior is not shown.
PICT_FRAME and AV_PICTURE_TYPE_B are constants not defined in the shown code; the frame-copy branch requires exact equality with the PICT_FRAME value.
The layout and first-dimension capacity of H264PredWeightTable (luma_weight/chroma_weight) are not declared in the shown code.
limitations: Out-of-bounds write at lines 70-74: with picture_structure == PICT_FRAME and ref_count[list] = 32, i = 31 produces index 16 + 2*31 + 1 = 79; ref_count[list] is unconstrained in the shown code and there is no protective check, but the array capacities are not identifiable from the shown code, so the boundary claim is unconfirmable and no CWE is attached.

Integer overflow of 16 + 2*i for ref_count[list] >= 2^30 is admitted by all shown guards, but the operand magnitude is not established within the shown code and the consequence depends on the unshown array capacity.

Resource exhaustion via a very large ref_count[list] (near-unbounded i loop) is not confirmed: ref_count is an internal-helper parameter and attacker control of its magnitude is not established within the shown code.
If the caller zero-initializes pwt (not shown), the uninitialized chroma_log2_weight_denom read reduces to a stale/default value; the shown code itself provides no such invariant.
Values at lines 15/19 clamp only line-10/12 results; they do not initialize chroma_log2_weight_denom on the chroma-absent path.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled SMTP path text of unchecked length is passed into the fixed-size struct mailaddr fields via text_to_mailaddr(line + 1), then its attacker-shaped tail is relocated by memmove(maddr->user, p, strlen(p)+1) with no length guard, enabling an out-of-bounds write and pre-auth remote code execution (CVE-2020-7247).

evidence.reason: Taint sink: the entry-point input line (residual range: any NUL-terminated string starting with '<' and containing '>', unbounded length, no length check anywhere in the shown code) is forwarded as line + 1 to text_to_mailaddr, which populates the fixed-size maddr->user/maddr->domain fields. The guard at L12-13 only requires the presence of '>', and L24 only requires a ':' in the local part, so a witness such as <a:BBBB...B> with a >255-byte tail passes every guard while carrying unbounded attacker text into the bounded buffer — the CVE-2020-7247 out-of-bounds write mechanism.

Size sink: the length argument strlen(p) + 1 is derived entirely from attacker-controlled local-part content (p = strchr(maddr->user, ':') + 1 at L23/L25). The ':' branch is attacker-selectable, so the guard at L24 admits the witness, and the post-colon tail of arbitrary attacker length is copied into maddr->user (assumed fixed 256-byte capacity per OpenSMTPD's struct mailaddr), overflowing it — primary CWE-787 out-of-bounds write leading to remote code execution.

assumptions: struct mailaddr's user and domain fields are fixed-size char arrays (256 bytes each in OpenSMTPD 6.4-6.6.1); the exact capacity is not declared in the shown snippet.
line is a NUL-terminated string supplied by the SMTP receive path, as required for strchr/strlen to terminate.
limitations: The body of text_to_mailaddr is not shown; the precise point at which the fixed-size user buffer is overfilled relies on its name-implied parse-into-fixed-fields semantics, capping confidence at 0.7.

If text_to_mailaddr truncated and NUL-terminated the local part within capacity, the shown memmove alone would stay in bounds; safety cannot be concluded because no shown check bounds the length reaching L20/L26.
NULL dereference of args (L18) or maddr (L20 onward) is not producible inside the shown code; it would require an out-of-scope caller passing NULL.
An unbounded scan by strchr(line, '>') (L12) beyond the receive buffer would require a missing NUL terminator, an invariant established only by the caller, not in the shown code.
Silent truncation of domain by strlcpy (L39-40) is intended and re-validated at L43; no security impact confirmed.

verdict.summary: unix_getpw dereferences encrypted_pass at line 137 without a NULL check. encrypted_pass is derived from pwd->pw_passwd (line 46), spwd->sp_pwdp (line 63), or fd_encrypt (line 33) — library/OS data the shown code never constrains and whose NULL possibility the code itself acknowledges at line 59 ((encrypted_pass == NULL) || ...). An attacker who sends a User-Name (line 27) for an account whose password field pointer is NULL drives encrypted_pass to NULL and the read at line 137 crashes the process (NULL pointer dereference, availability DoS).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled User-Name (line 27) selects the passwd/shadow entry whose password field is assigned to encrypted_pass at lines 46/63/33 with no NULL check; the guard at line 59 explicitly admits encrypted_pass == NULL but only routes it into the shadow lookup, and line 63 re-assigns encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp without re-validating, leaving NULL in the residual range up to the sink. Line 137 reads encrypted_pass[0] with no NULL guard, so any account whose libc/OS reports a NULL password pointer (an in-range value by the shown code's own admission at line 59) yields a NULL dereference, crashing the module/process: CWE-476.

assumptions: HAVE_GETSPNAM is typical on Linux/shadow-based systems; the NULL path was analyzed for the compiled configurations reachable in the shown preprocessor branches (OSFC2, plain getpwnam, and getpwnam+getspnam).
request->username->vp_strvalue is a non-NULL C string for a string User-Name attribute (framework invariant not established inside the shown code).
Empty password fields render as NULL on some libc/OS implementations; glibc renders them as empty strings, making the crash platform-dependent.
limitations: Log injection (CWE-117) candidate: unsanitized name (line 27) containing newlines/control characters reaches radlog/radlog_request (lines 39, 76-77, 95-96, 108, 116, 127); it survives to the log call, but the log backend's sanitization is outside the shown code and the impact is log forging only, so it is not reported as a confirmed finding.

pairfree(&vp) after pairmove(vp_list, &vp) (lines 143-144) would only be a use-after-free if the unshown pairmove fails to null its source; standard FreeRADIUS pairmove semantics null the source, so this is not confirmed from the shown code.
Expiry arithmetic (spwd->sp_lstchg + spwd->sp_max, line 107) could in principle overflow, but both operands come from the root-controlled shadow file, not attacker input.
The 10-character crypt-hash heuristic at line 59 is an authorization design choice (NULL/short fields forced through shadow lookup), not a confirmed bypass.
No memory-copy, size, index, or format-string inputs exist in the shown code; the only confirmed failure is the unguarded dereference at line 137.

verdict.summary: On the descriptor/getter error paths, className and attributeName are forwarded unescaped into fprintf(stderr,...) via %s (lines 7 and 12). No shown code strips CR/LF, so a value containing newlines can forge or split stderr log records: log injection, CWE-117.

evidence.snippet: fprintf(stderr, "Private script error: Target DOM attribute getter was not found. (Class name = %s, Attribute name = %s)\n", className, attributeName);
evidence.reason: className and attributeName are internal-helper parameters whose residual range the shown code leaves fully unconstrained (no NULL/length/content checks), and %s emits them verbatim, preserving embedded CR/LF. The line-6 guard (ToLocal failure or non-object descriptor) admits any parameter content, so e.g. attributeName="x\nFORGED" on a missing property reaches this stderr sink intact, splitting/forging the log record — CWE-117 primary mechanism.

evidence.snippet: fprintf(stderr, "Private script error: Target DOM attribute getter was not found. (Class name = %s, Attribute name = %s)\n", className, attributeName);
evidence.reason: Identical sink reached through the line-11 guard (descriptor's "get" missing or not a function), which likewise constrains only descriptor shape, not className/attributeName content; the newline-bearing attributeName still reaches the stderr log unchanged via %s — CWE-117.

assumptions: RELEASE_NOTREACHED() at lines 8 and 13 terminates execution in every build, so control never falls through to use an empty descriptor/getter Local.
fprintf %s follows standard C semantics: it copies bytes to the stream until NUL without escape processing.
limitations: Format-string injection (CWE-134) is absent: the format strings at lines 7 and 12 are compile-time literals; className/attributeName are always passed as %s arguments, never as the format string.

If classObjectOfPrivateScript (line 4) could return an empty Local, the call at line 6 would dereference it; the callee body and its failure semantics are not shown, so this and its attacker reachability are unconfirmed.

A renderer crash via RELEASE_NOTREACHED() (lines 8, 13) would be a DoS only if the missing-descriptor/getter state were attacker-triggerable; the shown registry-based lookup does not demonstrate such a path.

The attacker-controlled provenance of className/attributeName follows from their unconstrained internal-helper role in the shown code; no caller code is shown proving an external path injects these values, and whether stderr is consumed by a security-monitoring log is an external invariant.
rethrowExceptionInPrivateScript (line 19) forwards the same unescaped strings into exception messages, but its body is not shown, so any additional sink there is unverified.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in op_format: every caller-derived value reaches a status-checked call (u_save FAIL early-return at lines 11-13), a bounded cursor operation (line 34 guard, line 50 check_cursor), or a void helper whose consumer is not shown. No memory, injection, crypto, or authz sink exists in the shown code, so residual-range concerns cannot be converted into a confirmed finding.

assumptions: linenr_T is a signed long, so oap->start.lnum - 1 and oap->end.lnum + 1 cannot wrap for buffer-valid line numbers.
curbuf, curwin, and the win_T list are valid framework-provided objects while op_format runs.
u_save's OK/FAIL outcomes are both handled: FAIL exits at line 13.
limitations: oap->start.lnum - 1 can be 0 (start.lnum == 1) and oap->end.lnum + 1 can reach ml_line_count + 1; u_save's acceptance of these boundaries is not visible here, only its FAIL status, which is checked (lines 11-13), so no out-of-domain effect is confirmable.

oap->start/end/cursor_start are not validated in the shown code; extreme values only reach status-checked u_save or cursor code later bounded by check_cursor(), so no sink converts them into a memory-safety or injection failure.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable from the shown code. The only array store (algIds[algCount++] = alg, line 11) is guarded by the line 6 condition algCount < NUMOF_CIPHERS, which admits indices 0..NUMOF_CIPHERS-1, and the actual capacity of algIds is not declared in the shown code, so no boundary claim can be substantiated. The long-to-int narrowing at line 11 can corrupt a stored ALG_ID value on LP64, but the corrupted value is not consumed by an allocation-size, index, length, or pointer-arithmetic sink within the shown code (it is forwarded to Schannel outside this function), so it fails the confirmation standard.

assumptions: ciphers is a NUL-terminated C string; strtol/strchr/strncmp rely on that standard contract.
algIds has at least NUMOF_CIPHERS elements, matching the guard on line 6 by name (the constant's value and the array's actual size are not visible in the shown code).
get_alg_id_by_name returns 0 for an unrecognized name, consistent with its use at lines 8-10.
schannel_cred and algIds are non-NULL; the shown code cannot produce NULL for them.
limitations: Out-of-bounds write at algIds[algCount++] (line 11) is unconfirmable: the guard admits only indices 0..NUMOF_CIPHERS-1, and the real capacity of algIds is not identifiable from the shown code, so no exact excess can be demonstrated.

Long-to-int narrowing at line 11 (CWE-681-shaped) can wrap, e.g. ciphers='4294967295' on LP64 yields -1, but the corrupted value is a data element stored for later consumption by Schannel (lines 23-24 forward only the pointer and count); it never reaches an allocation-size, index, length, or pointer-arithmetic sink inside the shown code, so the impact is unconfirmed.
strtol (line 7) does not consume the whole token ('123abc' is accepted as 123) and its ERANGE overflow is not checked; this is a validation weakness with no traced memory-safety impact.

Silent truncation: if more than NUMOF_CIPHERS valid tokens are supplied, the loop exits at line 6 and line 25 still returns CURLE_OK; a trailing USE_STRONG_CRYPTO token would then never set the flag (line 16). This is a config-integrity/robustness concern (potentially CWE-754), but the cipher list is caller-chosen policy rather than attacker-derived data in the shown code, so it is not reported as a vulnerability.
The 18/21-byte strncmp prefix matches (lines 12-15) accept tokens like 'USE_STRONG_CRYPTOX' and set the flag without an exact token-boundary check; benign in the shown code.
NULL dereference of schannel_cred or algIds is possible only from an out-of-scope caller; the shown code has no NULL-producing path.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. qemu_register_machine allocates a type name with g_strconcat, registers a stack-local TypeInfo, frees the name buffer, and returns 0. The only dangerous-looking step is freeing 'name' (line 11) after handing it to type_register (line 10); whether that is a use-after-free depends entirely on callee retention behavior not visible in the shown code, and the pattern is the canonical QEMU type-registration idiom in which the TypeInfo (including the name) is duplicated during registration. Remaining concerns (NULL m/m->name, unbounded name length, discarded type_register return) lack a confirmable sink path entirely inside the shown code.

assumptions: m and m->name are valid per caller contract; the shown code imposes no guard on them.
g_strconcat/g_new abort on allocation failure (standard glib semantics), so the line-3 result cannot be a NULL returned to the shown path.
type_register consumes/duplicates the TypeInfo fields during the call; otherwise the stack-allocated struct at line 4 would itself dangle, contradicting the canonical QEMU idiom this code implements.
limitations: Potential use-after-free of 'name' (lines 3/5/10/11) if type_register retained the pointer without copying; the callee body is not shown, so retention cannot be confirmed or a concrete overrun/witness derived from the shown code.
NULL dereference of m->name at line 3 if the caller passes NULL/invalid m; NULL is not produced anywhere in the shown code and can only be supplied out of scope.
Unbounded m->name length passed to g_strconcat (line 3): the shown code imposes no cap, but no sink or loop consumes a derived size, index, or length, and glib handles the concatenation internally.

Discarded return of type_register (line 10) and unconditional return 0 (line 12): no shown step has a distinguishable failure status, so no error-handling flaw is confirmable (CWE-390/754 not established).

verdict.summary: mov_read_stsz takes the sample-count field (entries) directly from the file and constrains it only against multiplication overflow (line 11). A crafted stsz atom with sample_size=0 and a large entries value passes the guard and drives av_malloc(entries*sizeof(long)) (up to ~4 GiB on 64-bit) plus an unbound read loop of up to ~536M get_be32 iterations with no relationship to the atom's actual size, enabling denial of service via a tiny input file (CWE-770).

evidence.reason: entries is attacker-controlled (get_be32 at line 10) with residual range 0..0x1FFFFFFE on LP64 after the line-11 guard, which only prevents integer overflow and admits e.g. entries=1,000,000. The resulting 8 MiB (up to ~4 GiB) allocation is driven by a file that need not contain any sample-size data, exhausting heap/memory without an input-length bound; primary mechanism is CWE-770 uncontrolled resource allocation.

The loop bound is the attacker-supplied entries value admitted by the line-11 guard (e.g., 1,000,000 < 536,870,911 with sample_size=0 at line 17). No check ties entries to the atom size or remaining file bytes, so a 12-byte file forces 1,000,000 get_be32 iterations (each reading EOF as 0), and the maximum admitted count yields ~2.1 billion byte-read calls; CPU/latency are unbounded by input volume, confirming CWE-770 uncontrolled resource consumption at this read sink.

assumptions: LP64 target: sizeof(long)=8 and size_t is 64-bit, so UINT_MAX/sizeof(long) = 0x1FFFFFFF; the arithmetic guard is also sound on ILP32 (0x3FFFFFFE * 4 fits unsigned 32-bit).
ByteIOContext get_byte/get_be32 return 0 at EOF (standard FFmpeg semantics), so reading past the atom end yields zeros rather than memory corruption.

av_malloc succeeds for moderate attacker-chosen sizes (e.g., 8 MiB), which is ordinary behavior on standard 64-bit systems; huge sizes may fail and return -1, which only limits the CPU component of the DoS.
limitations: Line 3 (c->fc->streams[c->fc->nb_streams-1]) would be an out-of-bounds read if nb_streams==0, but the invariant that at least one stream exists before stsz parsing is established by the caller, not in the shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.
The line-11 guard correctly prevents integer overflow in entries*sizeof(long) on both 32-bit and 64-bit builds; no CWE-190/CWE-787 memory-corruption finding is justified in this code.
Reading sample sizes beyond the atom/file end is a robustness/correctness issue (all-zero sizes) with no memory-safety impact under the assumed ByteIOContext EOF behavior.
On systems where av_malloc fails for very large entries, the function returns -1 and the loop is not executed; the confirmed DoS relies on moderate entries whose allocation succeeds.

verdict.summary: In mov_read_stsz, the attacker-controlled 32-bit entry count is stored in a signed int and used as the allocation size entries*sizeof(long) without any cap. On 32-bit targets the multiplication wraps (e.g., entries=0x40000001 yields size 4), av_malloc succeeds, and the loop writes up to 2^31 long-sized samples, causing a heap-buffer-overflow write (CWE-787) rooted in the integer overflow (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: entries originates at line 10 as get_be32(pb), an attacker-controlled uint32 narrowed to int with residual range [INT_MIN, INT_MAX] and no validation in the shown code. The guard at line 15 (sample_size==0) admits the continuation path. With entries=0x40000001 and sizeof(long)=4 (32-bit size_t), entries*sizeof(long) wraps mod 2^32 to 4, so av_malloc receives a 4-byte size while the loop at line 21 will write entries elements; this corrupted allocation size is the CWE-190 root cause feeding the CWE-787 write.

The loop at line 20 admits i in [0, entries-1] with entries=0x40000001 (member of the admitted sets of guards at lines 15 and 18), while the object allocated at line 17 has only 4 bytes on a 32-bit target due to the wrap. At i=1 the write of sizeof(long)=4 bytes lands at byte offset 4..7, 4 bytes past capacity, with the excess growing to ~4 GiB; this is a heap-buffer-overflow write (CWE-787) from a crafted MOV stsz atom.

assumptions: The exploited wrap requires a 32-bit target where sizeof(long)==4 and size_t is 32-bit; on a 64-bit target entries<=2^31-1 yields entries*8<=2^34, which does not wrap and keeps the loop in bounds.
av_malloc(4) succeeds and returns non-NULL so the guard at line 18 admits the continuation path.
limitations: Line 3 (streams[nb_streams-1]) OOB read when nb_streams==0 is unconfirmable: nb_streams is an internal-helper/provenance input and the shown code provides no guard or invariant establishing reachability of nb_streams==0.

On 64-bit platforms the remaining concern is an attacker-controlled allocation up to ~17 GB (entries near 2^31) with clean NULL-handling; a DoS-only claim depends on unchecked allocation/overcommit behavior and is not confirmed.
Negative entries (unsigned >= 0x80000000) convert to a huge size_t, av_malloc fails, and the NULL check at lines 18-19 returns -1, so no memory-safety sink is reached on that path.
Truncated input makes get_be32 return 0 silently, filling sample_sizes with zeros (data-integrity only, no memory impact in the shown code).
sample_count may hold a negative or huge value that other (unshown) code could consume; out of scope for this snippet.

verdict.summary: No confirmed exploitable vulnerability. The only memory sink, algIds[algCount++] (line 11), is protected by the loop guard algCount < 45 (line 6) which admits indices 0..44 against a capacity of 45 (line 5); the iteration strictly advances startCur each pass, so the loop terminates for all inputs. Parser quirks (strtol without endptr on line 7 misparsing tokens such as "3DES-CBC-SHA" to 3, negative or overflowed values being stored as ALG_ID on line 11, and silent truncation of lists longer than 45 entries with a CURLE_OK return) cause only incorrect cipher configuration, not a memory-safety or identity/authorization failure, and are recorded as limitations.

limitations: strtol at line 7 is called with endptr=NULL and errno ignored: digit-leading names are misparsed (e.g., "3DES-CBC-SHA" yields 3) and partial hex prefixes are accepted (e.g., "0x13AES" yields 0x13AE), writing unintended ALG_ID values at line 11; impact is limited to incorrect cipher configuration because the cipher list is user-selected by design and no security boundary is crossed, so no CWE is confirmed.

The flag names are matched by prefix (strncmp, lines 12-15), so tokens like "USE_STRONG_CRYPTOjunk" are accepted; this is lenient parsing with no security impact.

Whether get_alg_id_by_name (line 9) misuses the full remaining substring (which extends past the current token to the string's NUL) depends entirely on its unshown body and is not analyzed as a finding.

verdict.summary: my_strdup allocates strlen(str) bytes (line 12) but strcpy writes strlen(str)+1 bytes including the NUL terminator (line 16), causing a deterministic one-byte heap out-of-bounds write for any argv[1] input (e.g., "aa").

Line 12 sizes the heap allocation to N = strlen(str), so the buffer capacity is N bytes; strcpy at line 16 writes N+1 bytes (string plus terminator). Witness "aa": allocation of 2 bytes, write of 3 bytes — terminator write at index 2 == capacity, a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Guards at line 7 (non-NULL str) and line 13 (non-NULL malloc result) both admit the witness and impose no size constraint.

assumptions: argv[1] is NUL-terminated per the C standard's argv contract, which also guarantees that strlen/strcpy terminate.
An empty-string input (N=0) also overflows (strcpy writes 1 byte into the malloc(0) object), but the non-empty witness "aa" makes the claim independent of malloc(0) semantics.
limitations: If malloc fails, my_strdup returns NULL and main's printf("%s", copy) at line 30 passes NULL as a %s argument — undefined behavior (glibc prints "(null)"; other libcs may crash). This requires an allocation failure and is a single-shot DoS only, so it is demoted with no CWE.
The missing newline in printf at line 30 is a cosmetic issue, not a security finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmable vulnerability in SProcXkbSelectEvents as shown. The byte-swap reads at lines 56-61 are executed only after the capacity guard at lines 53-54 (dataLeft >= size*2), REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE at line 6 prevents unsigned underflow of dataLeft at line 23, and the mask walk at lines 24-28 is bounded to at most 16 terminating iterations because maskLeft is CARD16-derived with bit 1 pre-cleared. No OOB access, injection, weak-crypto, file, or error-handling flaw survives these guards.

client->req_len is maintained in host byte order by the dispatch layer and is consistent with the byte-swapped stuff->length at line 5; the only external invariant relied on is that line 6 rejects undersized requests.
swaps/swapl are in-place CARD16/CARD32 byte swaps that read and write exactly the width of their argument.
XkbMapNotify == 1, so `~XkbMapNotifyMask` clears bit 1 from maskLeft at line 24; affectWhich is CARD16 with residual range 0..0xFFFF after the swaps at lines 7-12.
limitations: ProcXkbSelectEvents (line 75) is not shown; its internal handling of the byte-swapped data is outside the scope of this analysis.
The 1-2 trailing bytes tolerated by line 69 (dataLeft > 2) are never read, so they cannot cause out-of-bounds access within this function.

If the guard at lines 53-54 were placed below the swaps/swapl calls at lines 56-61, an out-of-bounds read/write of up to 8 bytes past the request data would be reachable; that ordering is not present in the shown code.

Because affectWhich is CARD16, bits above bit 15 cannot be set, so the bit<<=1 at line 25 cannot wrap while maskLeft is non-zero; if the field were wider, an adversarial mask could stall or overflow the loop.
Whether a 2-byte surplus is protocol-legal is a functional question only; it has no security effect here.

verdict.summary: In parse_mb_skip, the SKIP_TYPE_ROW and SKIP_TYPE_COL branches verify only one remaining bit (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1) before reading the per-row/per-column flag, but when the flag is 0 the nested loop performs mb_width (ROW) or mb_height (COL) further get_bits1 reads with no budget check. A truncated stream with exactly one bit left at the guard admits an out-of-bounds read past the end of the bitstream's valid data (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Sink for the ROW over-read: the guard at line 24 admits get_bits_left >= 1 and the flag read at line 26 consumes the verified bit; when the flag is 0 the loop at line 31 executes mb_width iterations, each calling get_bits1 at line 33 with no additional budget test. Witness: skip_type=ROW, mb_height=1, mb_width=2, stream ending after the flag bit 0 leaves get_bits_left==1 (member of the admitted set {>=1}); two bit-reads then proceed past size_in_bits, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) of the bitstream buffer; excess = mb_width bits beyond the last valid bit.

Sink for the COL over-read, symmetric to the ROW case: guard at line 39 admits get_bits_left >= 1, flag read at line 41 consumes the last verified bit, and when the flag is 0 the loop at line 46 performs mb_height get_bits1 calls at line 48 with no budget check. Witness: skip_type=COL, mb_width=1, mb_height=2, stream ending after the flag bit 0 (get_bits_left==1); two bit-reads proceed past the end of the bitstream (CWE-125); excess = mb_height bits beyond valid data.

assumptions: get_bits/get_bits1 advance the GetBitContext position by 1 bit per bit read and, per FFmpeg's standard semantics, read from the buffer mapped by size_in_bits, so reads beyond the remaining budget access data past the valid bitstream.
Loops over mb_width/mb_height execute only when those values are positive; the shown code imposes no constraint on them, so mb_width/mb_height >= 1 is assumed for the witnessed loops.
The 2-bit get_bits at line 6 can select every switch case (SKIP_TYPE_NONE/MPEG/ROW/COL), making the ROW and COL branches reachable from attacker-controlled input.
limitations: The physical heap over-read beyond the allocation boundary is not fully confirmable from the shown code: the underlying buffer capacity and AV_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE are not visible here, and for typical WMV2 resolutions the ~mb_width/mb_height-bit over-read may remain inside zero padding; with CONFIG_SAFE_BITSTREAM_READER the physical read is suppressed (logical over-consumption remains).
The mb_type write index at lines 11/19/28/32/43/47 cannot be confirmed as an OOB write because mb_type's allocation size and the mb_width <= mb_stride invariant are not established in the shown code.

Integer overflow of s->mb_height * s->mb_width at line 15 (and of mb_y * s->mb_stride in the write index) requires dimensions set in codec initialization outside the shown code; no in-function bound exists, so the overflow and its consequences are unconfirmed.

verdict.summary: In jpc_pi_nextrpcl, pi->prcno is computed from image-geometry-derived loop positions (lines 66-72) and used to index pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos (line 77), followed by *prclyrno read (line 78) and ++(*prclyrno) write (line 79). The only bound on prcno is assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs) (line 74), which is compiled out under NDEBUG. A witness with x = numhprcs, y = numvprcs-1 passes every functional guard (x < xend, y < yend, numprcs != 0, and the modulo condition with rpx=rpy=0) and yields prcno == numprcs (index == capacity), causing an out-of-bounds heap read, and a heap write when the OOB value <= lyrno.

The witness x=numhprcs, y=numvprcs-1, xend=numhprcs+1, yend=numvprcs gives prcno==numprcs==capacity; the only guard, assert at line 74, is removed under NDEBUG, so the index reaches one-past-end.

Sink: out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787) on ++(*prclyrno) when the one-past-end value read at line 78 is <= lyrno (0 on first iteration, typical for zeroed/small heap contents); reachable because line 74's assert is compiled out under NDEBUG and no functional bounds check on pi->prcno exists in the shown code.

assumptions: Release build defines NDEBUG, so the standard assert macro at line 74 is compiled out; with assertions enabled the same witness instead triggers an abort at line 74 (reachable-assertion DoS, not memory corruption).
prclyrnos is allocated with numprcs int elements (indices 0..numprcs-1), as implied by its per-precinct semantics and by the assert invariant at line 74 naming numprcs as the bound.

pchg->rlvlnostart/rlvlnoend/compnostart/compnoend/lyrnoend are non-negative and no more than numlyrs/numcomps/maxrlvls as the iterator setup requires; the shown code itself guarantees only the loop guards.

Negative pi->rlvlno from a negative pchg->rlvlnostart would index pi->picomp->pirlvls[pi->rlvlno] (line 53) out of bounds, but no witness for a negative rlvlnostart exists in the shown code.
Modulo-by-zero at lines 43/45 if pi->xstep/pi->ystep remain 0 (e.g., numcomps==0) is an internal-consistency concern with no attacker-controlled reachability shown.

Signed int overflow/UB of pi->prcno (line 72), of picomp->hsamp*(1<<...) (lines 29-32), and shifts by attacker-influenced exponents (lines 29-32, 60-70) lack concrete magnitude bounds and witnesses within the shown code.

NULL pchg dereference at lines 19/40 and CWE-125 as a separate entry are not reported: the read at line 78 shares the same missing-check root cause as the write, and NULL pchg is not producible inside the shown code.

verdict.summary: my_strdup follows the standard strdup pattern: it sizes the heap allocation as strlen(str)+1 (line 17), checks malloc failure (line 18) and NULL input (line 12), and strcpy (line 21) writes exactly strlen(str)+1 bytes into a buffer of exactly that capacity (max index strlen < capacity). In main, argv[1] is NUL-terminated and guarded by argc==2 (line 30), printf uses literal format strings (lines 31, 39), and copy is freed exactly once (line 40). No attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, crypto, or access-control vulnerability is confirmed; remaining concerns (size_t wrap of strlen+1, exit code 0 on allocation failure, stdlib.h include ordering) are theoretical or non-security-relevant and are recorded in limitations.

assumptions: argv[1] is a NUL-terminated string per standard host-environment semantics for argv, so strlen and strcpy terminate on it; this invariant is the foundation of the shown code's safety and is not itself imposed by the shown code.
malloc failure is handled and does not occur for legitimate small allocations unless the platform is out of memory.
The file is compiled as a single translation unit as presented; any deviation from that ordering (e.g., implicit declaration of malloc before line 27) is a build-environment concern.

verdict.summary: In write_refcount_block_entries, no guard enforces last_index >= first_index (or any upper bound on the indices). A write length of that magnitude is out of the domain of a byte count for the small refcount-block cache buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read of the cache (heap disclosure/crash) inside the write path; primary mechanism is the signed-to-unsigned size conversion (CWE-195) corrupting the length at the sink.

assumptions: size_t is 64-bit (unsigned, modulo-2^64 conversion of negative int values).

With 32-bit size_t the product wraps modulo 2^32: numSpecs = 2^29 gives 2^29*8 == 0 (mod 2^32), so bytes_to_int32(0 + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq) == 2 matches a 2-word request, admitting a length that supplies zero spec bytes while the claimed count is 2^29. This admitted set intersects the failure set of the guard; the wrapped value then drives the allocation/copy guarded at lines 12-15, making integer overflow the root cause of the length-check bypass (CWE-190).

This is the consumer of the attacker-derived count: the specs buffer is allocated from data located at (char*) stuff + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq, sized by the numSpecs-based product admitted at line 10. Under the wrapped admission (length=2, numSpecs=2^29) the request supplies no spec entries but the consumer processes the claimed 2^29 entries, causing attempted oversized allocation (BadAlloc/DoS) or unbounded downstream iteration/OOB access, i.e. the CWE-190 wrap reaches a memory/allocation sink.

verdict.summary: qcrypto_cipher_decrypt forwards the length parameter to nettle decrypt calls with no validation that it is a multiple of the cipher block size. nettle's AES/DES decrypt functions and cbc_decrypt assert length % block_size == 0 and abort the process on violation, so any caller-supplied non-aligned length (e.g., 20 bytes with AES, block size 16) reaches a reachable assertion and terminates the process: a denial of service via missing input validation (CWE-617).

ctx->alg_decrypt(ctx->ctx_decrypt ? ctx->ctx_decrypt : ctx->ctx_encrypt,
                         len, out, in);

The same unconstrained len (residual range [0, SIZE_MAX], admitted by switch case QCRYPTO_CIPHER_MODE_CBC at line 13 with no length check) is passed as the length argument; the shown call also supplies ctx->niv as block_size. nettle's cbc_decrypt enters with assert(!(length % block_size)), so len=20 with ctx->niv=16 (AES) fails the assertion and aborts the process: CWE-617 reachable assertion, denial of service.

assumptions: ctx->alg_decrypt points to a nettle block-cipher decrypt (nettle_aes*_decrypt / DES wrapper) whose entry point asserts assert(!(length % block_size)) and aborts on violation; verified in nettle aes128/aes192/aes256-decrypt.c and in upstream QEMU commit 3a661f1eabf7e8db66e28489884d9b54aacb94ea ('nettle will abort').
The build is compiled without NDEBUG so assert() is live, which is QEMU's default configuration.

This is a predictable-salt flaw (CWE-760): identical passwords yield identical (hash, salt) pairs across users/databases, and a single precomputation attack over the one known salt defeats the purpose of per-user salting.

evidence.reason: The shown code deliberately chooses the salt: every iteration zero-fills all 32 salt bytes (the RAND_bytes call at lines 27-30 is commented out, leaving no randomness or per-user diversification). The zero-filled buffer is consumed as the salt argument of PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC at line 35, so the residual salt-value range is exactly {0x00 x 32} for every i and every invocation reachable from main (argc >= 3 at line 47 admits count >= 1, and no other guard alters the salt). Primary mechanism is CWE-760: a one-way hash with a predictable constant salt, enabling cross-user identical-password correlation and single-table precomputation.

assumptions: argv/argc are treated as attacker-controlled entry-point input; the only constraint enforced by the shown code is argc >= 3 (line 47), yielding count >= 1.
In main, usernames and passwords vectors are sized count (lines 53-54), so the loops at lines 57-60, 65-70 and the helper loop are in-bounds for the shown caller.

The vector capacity is not identifiable from inside the shown function and main always passes matching sizes, so this is unconfirmed with no CWE.

The tainted command string b is handed to r_core_undo_new as the apply-command of an undo pair and pushed at line 132; by the name-implied semantics of the undo API, the stored string is later re-executed as a radare2 command, at which point the surviving ';' runs the attacker-chosen commands. verdict.summary: No confirmable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in _php_mb_regex_ereg_replace_exec. Every input-derived size/index at a sink is bounded by a located guard (backref range check at lines 94-95, replacement length gates at lines 89 and 101, string-end gates at lines 115 and 122, negative-length gate at line 122), and region values from onig_search (lines 64-65) are bounded by that call's standard contract (0 <= beg[0] <= end[0] <= str.size(), beg[0] >= pos). Both search and replacement loops strictly advance and terminate on all inputs. Remaining concerns (unchecked onig_region_new() at line 62; unguarded use of regs->beg[0]/end[0] at lines 80-81 and 111-113; possible fwd==0 stall at lines 102-104) depend on OOM-only allocation failure or on callee behavior outside the shown code, so they are hardening concerns, not confirmed findings.

assumptions: onig_search, called with start=pos and range=string_lim (lines 64-65), fills the region only on success (err >= 0) and per its documented contract satisfies beg[0] >= start, beg[n] <= end[n], end[n] <= range == str.data()+str.size(), with unmatched groups set to -1.
onig_region_new() (line 62) allocates a fixed-size region whose failure is environmental OOM only; onig_search accepts a NULL region, and onig_region_free handles NULL
php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex(p, enc) (line 86) returns a character byte count >= 1 for any byte of the encoding named by enc.
PHP String::data()/size() are byte-based and StringBuffer::append copies exactly the given length.
limitations: regs from onig_region_new() (line 62) is used unchecked; if that fixed-size allocation failed, the success path would NULL-dereference at regs->beg[0]/num_regs/end[0] (lines 81, 93, 111). Not a finding because the allocation size is not attacker-controlled.

The pre-match append (lines 80-81) and pos update (lines 111-113) have no independent bounds check on regs->beg[0]/regs->end[0]; they rely on the onig_search contract. If the engine ever returned out-of-contract region values, lines 80-81 could form a negative/huge append length and line 113 could place pos past string_lim. Not confirmable from the shown code.
If php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex (line 86) ever returned 0, the replacement loop would not advance (lines 102-104) and would stall; the shown code has no zero check. Depends on callee semantics not shown.

verdict.summary: The only bound check, `if (end - start < nal_length_size)` at line 4, admits negative nal_length_size values because a non-negative buffer size is never less than a negative count. A value such as -1 then reaches `while (nal_length_size--)` at line 6, whose post-decrement condition (-1, -2, -3, ...) never becomes false, so the loop never terminates and line 7 (`res = (res << 8) | *start++;`) repeatedly dereferences past `end` (OOB read) while hanging the caller. No shown constraint imposes nal_length_size >= 0 or >= 1.

evidence.reason: nal_length_size's residual range after the only guard (line 4) includes every negative int: `end - start < nal_length_size` is false for any non-negative buffer size when the count is negative, so e.g. -1 passes. The post-decrement loop condition then evaluates -1 (truthy), -2 (truthy), ... and never reaches 0, so the loop has an unreachable exit condition (CWE-835) and the shown code never returns. The guard's admitted set is therefore insufficient; no check excludes the failing value.

With a negative nal_length_size admitted by line 4 (e.g., -1 with end - start = 10), this read executes for an unbounded number of iterations, dereferencing indices 10, 11, ... beyond the [start, end) object that line 4 was meant to bound. The read index is governed solely by the loop counter whose non-negativity is never checked, producing an out-of-bounds read (consequence of the same CWE-835 root cause: the loop never terminates because a negative counter decrements away from zero).

assumptions: end points one past the last valid byte of the buffer, as implied by the `end - start` size computation and `> end` boundary checks.
int is 32-bit, the common platform type; this matters only for the overflow notes in limitations.

nal_length_size provenance is unknown from the shown code; per the internal-helper role, only the residual range left by the shown guards is analyzed, so real callers may restrict it to 1..4 — that is outside the shown code and does not change the shown-code result.
limitations: For nal_length_size >= 5 with a sufficiently large buffer, `res = (res << 8) | *start++` performs signed left shifts past the int width (UB/overflow), but the corrupted res only feeds the `res < 0` check at line 8 and no index/size/allocation sink, so no exploitable corruption is confirmed (unconfirmed CWE-190).

For nal_length_size == 4 and a 4-byte length whose high bit is set, res becomes negative and line 8 returns NULL, rejecting valid unsigned AVCC lengths; this is a correctness regression with no memory-safety impact.

Line 8 evaluates `start + res > end` before `res < 0`, so pointer arithmetic outside the object may itself be technically UB for pathological res; both outcomes return NULL and no dereference occurs, so this is theoretical only.

The hang/OOB read requires a caller to pass a non-positive nal_length_size; since callers are not shown, end-user exploitability depends on whether an external input can reach this parameter, which cannot be established from the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: In virgl_cmd_get_capset, max_size returned by virgl_renderer_get_cap_set is bounded only by the nonzero check at line 10. In sizeof(*resp) + max_size at line 14, a 32-bit size_t addition wraps (max_size = 0xFFFFFFFF) yields a 23-byte allocation, and virgl_renderer_fill_caps at lines 16-18 then writes the max_size-byte capset into capset_data at offset 24, causing a guest-triggerable heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), with the integer wrap (CWE-190) as root cause.

evidence.reason: max_size (residual range [1, 2^32-1]; the only guard, !max_size at line 10, excludes just 0) flows into the allocation at line 14, which wraps on 32-bit size_t: max_size=0xFFFFFFFF gives a 23-byte buffer while capset_data sits at offset 24. fill_caps then writes the max_size-byte capset into that pointer, so every byte of the write is outside the allocation: heap OOB write, primary CWE-787, with the size wrap at line 14 as independent root cause CWE-190.

The allocation-size operand sizeof(*resp) + max_size is computed in size_t+uint32_t; on a 32-bit size_t build the addition is 32-bit and wraps for max_size >= 2^32 - sizeof(*resp) (witness 0xFFFFFFFF passes the line 10 guard, admitted set [1, 2^32-1]), producing a 23-byte allocation. The corrupted size is then consumed as the buffer whose capset_data region is passed to virgl_renderer_fill_caps at lines 16-18: integer overflow (CWE-190) feeding the heap overflow (CWE-787).

assumptions: The analyzed target build has a 32-bit size_t (ILP32), under which sizeof(*resp) + max_size wraps to a tiny value for max_size near UINT32_MAX; the shown code does not pin the platform's size_t width.
virgl_renderer_fill_caps fills the requested capset with max_size bytes, matching the size that virgl_renderer_get_cap_set reports for that capset (name-implied semantics).
limitations: The int return value of virgl_renderer_get_cap_set (lines 8-9) is discarded; if it can fail without writing max_size/max_ver, line 10 and line 14 would consume indeterminate values, but the callee failure semantics are not visible in the shown code (CWE-754/457 unconfirmable).
g_malloc failure (line 14) would abort the process (glib semantics) rather than return NULL, so no NULL-dereference path is producible inside the shown code.
On 64-bit size_t builds the addition does not wrap; there only an up-to-4GiB allocation remains whose size is determined by the host library, not by guest-controlled values in the shown code.
The response at line 19 reuses the same wrapped length, so the copy itself matches the small allocation (no independent OOB read); the guest only receives a truncated caps payload.

Crashes in get_entrypoint itself or in memory allocators it may call are outside the shown code and are not assessed here.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime discards the return status of inflate() at lines 12 and 29 (and deflate() at line 19) and unconditionally returns 0, so an attacker-supplied compressed stream that fails to decompress is reported as success and the partial or stale tmpblock is retained as the primed reference block (CWE-754, unchecked exceptional condition / success after failure).

evidence.reason: src and size are unconstrained in the shown code (lines 8-9 impose no validation), so any byte string/length is admitted; a non-zlib stream makes inflate return Z_DATA_ERROR under standard zlib semantics and the return value is discarded. Execution continues to lines 16-29 and returns 0 at line 30, so the partial/stale tmpblock is treated as a successfully primed reference block: CWE-754 (improper check of an exceptional condition, success reported after failure).

The second inflate consumes the attacker-derived deflate_block data (avail_in set at line 26 from deflate output length) and its return status is again discarded; the function then returns 0 at line 30 regardless, so a decompression failure or no-progress condition is silently accepted as a successful prime, continuing the CWE-754 error-handling flaw.

assumptions: s->zstream was previously initialized by inflateInit by the caller, as required for inflateReset at line 21 to succeed (standard zlib API semantics).
avail_in and avail_out are zlib's uInt (unsigned 32-bit) types per the zlib public API used at lines 8-29.
limitations: A negative size (int, line 9) converts to a huge uInt avail_in at the inflate read sink (line 12), a CWE-195/CWE-125 candidate, but the allocated capacity of src is not identifiable from the shown code, so the exact out-of-bounds excess cannot be confirmed.

s->block_size * 3 at lines 11, 16, and 28 can overflow if block_size is a large signed int, corrupting avail_out/avail_in at the zlib length sinks, but block_size's declared type/range and the capacities of tmpblock and deflate_block are not present in the shown code, so the overflow-to-OOB chain is unconfirmable.

If the first inflate (line 12) fails before producing output, deflate (line 19) re-compresses stale or uninitialized tmpblock contents; the downstream security impact of using that data as the reference block is outside the shown code.

If deflate_block_size is too small for the flushed input, deflate (line 19) drops unconsumed input and line 26 feeds only produced bytes, a data-integrity/truncation flaw whose security impact is not demonstrated in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The WEB branch embeds attacker-influenced text into a JavaScript snippet executed via emscripten_run_script, but the only character that can close the single-quoted JS string literal (0x27) is fully excluded by the strchr guard at line 8; no string in the guard's admitted set can break out of the literal, so no code injection is reachable. Residual issues (trailing backslash or raw newline causing a JS syntax error, NULL input) are robustness/out-of-scope concerns, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

The internal implementation of `TextFormat` (buffer sizing, truncation) is not shown; no overflow or format-string claim about that callee can be confirmed from the shown code.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime ignores the return values of both inflate() calls (lines 14 and 31) and unconditionally returns success (line 32). An attacker-controlled, non-NULL src containing bytes that are not a valid zlib stream (e.g., a single 0x00 byte with size=1) makes the first inflate fail with Z_DATA_ERROR; the code still runs the rest of the priming sequence on the failed z_stream and reports success, leaving the decoder's compression state unprimed/errored and proceeding as if priming succeeded (CWE-754). No in-function memory corruption is demonstrated; impact is bounded to silent failure/DoS via crafted media input.

evidence.reason: The return status of inflate is discarded. src's contents are arbitrary non-NULL bytes (the only guard, line 5, checks only for NULL), so the witness src={0x00}, size=1 passes every guard on the path (lines 5, 15, 23) and deterministically makes inflate return Z_DATA_ERROR (not Z_OK/Z_STREAM_END). Control continues to line 18 (derived avail_in), line 21 (deflate), line 28, and line 32 'return 0', reporting success after the failed decompression step — the error-handling flaw (CWE-754).

Second unchecked inflate on the same z_stream after the first inflate failed: the stream is in an error state and the input at line 28 is derived from the failed run (avail_in = deflate_block_size - zs.avail_out, which is 0/empty when the first inflate produced nothing), so this call also fails (Z_BUF_ERROR/Z_DATA_ERROR) and the discarded status again lets the function reach 'return 0' at line 32. Same CWE-754 mechanism at a distinct sink statement.

s->zstream was initialised with inflateInit by the (not shown) caller before flashsv2_prime runs; tmpblock/deflate_block are valid, non-NULL allocations.
Call-site confirmation relies on the standard name/contract of inflate (its return value carries decompression failures); no callee body is needed.
limitations: Negative size (int->uInt at line 11) would make avail_in ~2^32-1 and could cause an OOB read inside inflate from src, but the capacity of the src buffer is not identifiable from the shown code and no shown caller can be shown to pass a negative size; boundary claim unconfirmable (no CWE assigned).

s->block_size * 3 (lines 13, 18, 30) could overflow int and yield a huge avail_out if block_size > INT_MAX/3, but block_size's provenance/range and the capacities of s->tmpblock/s->deflate_block are not shown, so any overflow/OOB claim is unconfirmable.

deflate (line 21) return is discarded; if produced tmpblock bytes exceed deflate_block_size, output is truncated (Z_BUF_ERROR) and the remainder is dropped by deflateEnd (line 22) — silent truncation without demonstrated security impact.
No loops exist in the shown code, so there are no iteration-bound/sentinel/read-position invariants to verify.

The concrete post-failure harm (crash/garbage decode in the caller) is outside the shown code; within the shown code the impact is limited to the false-success error-handling path, which is why severity is low.
